Keep the array busy

A 16×16 output-stationary array. Blue and red operands enter skewed, the amber wavefront crosses the die, and green accumulators fill.

The core insights

Everything in the four PDFs, boiled down. If you only read one page, read this one. Each insight links to the chapter that proves it.

Source tags used throughout: J Jouppi, Lakshmanamurthy, Young and Patterson, the Ironwood paper. R Bjarke Roune, Designing AI Chip Hardware and Software. IA Irrational Analysis, It's the dataflow, stupid (an unfinished draft). E the Component Encyclopedia. F your own factbook in research/. D derived here and tested in deep_dive/model/. O outside the four PDFs: general engineering knowledge you should re-check against a real PDK.

What a chip actually is

1. An AI chip is a machine for keeping a systolic array busy. The array sets the ceiling on speed and efficiency. Everything else on the die exists to feed it, drain it, or do the small amount of work it cannot do. Brand names like TensorCore, MXU, Matrix Core and NeuronCore all refer to the same idea. R → Systolic arrays

2. Any computer can be compared with four questions. How is memory arranged? How does compute reach memory? How fancy and how wide is the compute? How do chips talk to each other? Use these before you read any spec sheet. IA → The frame

3. The goal is balance, measured in useful work per dollar or per watt. Peak FLOPS is one input. A real design balances systolic compute, vector compute, scalar compute, memory bandwidth, memory capacity, network bandwidth, thermals and latency all at once. Adding compute to a chip that is not compute-bound only lowers utilization. R → The frame

4. Data movement is the cost you are really managing. An HBM byte costs on the order of 100 times the energy of an 8-bit multiply-accumulate. Every architecture decision is about how many times you can reuse a byte before you have to fetch another one. O → Area, clock, power

Why arrays have the size and shape they do

5. Doubling an array's side divides scalar work by 4 and vector work by 2. A 2N×2N array does four times the math of an N×N array with vectors only twice as wide. Going from Volta's 4×4 to a TPU's 128×128 is five doublings: 1024× less scalar work and 32× less vector work per unit of matmul. This is why a 30-person TPU team could compete with Nvidia. R → Systolic arrays

6. The reduction depth K is the hard limit on array size. You can usually find more rows or more columns of work by batching. You cannot invent more terms in a dot product. Attention has K around 16 to 128 while feed-forward has K in the thousands, so attention is what stops arrays from being 1024×1024. R → Matmul shape

7. Every factor of two of mismatch costs you a factor of two or four. A 64-wide problem on a 128-wide array runs at 25%, or 50% if software packs it block-diagonally. A 257 dimension can run at half the speed of a 256 dimension. Padding is the tax on shape mismatch. R → Matmul shape

8. The row count needed for full utilization equals the array's width, divided by how much more bandwidth weights get than activations. On a 128×128 array with equal bandwidth, you need 128 rows of activations per weight tile. One row gets 0.8% utilization. This is the single most important equation in inference hardware, because those rows are your batch. RD → Matmul shape

9. Bigger arrays force bigger batches, which force more KV cache and more latency, which force faster networks. Array size is not a local decision. It propagates through batch, HBM capacity, token latency and link bandwidth. R → Scale-out

10. A larger array clocked down is still more efficient than a smaller array at the same throughput, up to a limit. Keep this option in your search even when you do not need more FLOPS. Lower clocks allow lower voltages, and dynamic energy falls with voltage squared. RO → Area, clock, power

11. Numerics are the cheapest speedup you will ever get, and they are not free. Going from 16 to 8 bits halves bandwidth and more than halves multiplier cost. Below 8 bits, the accumulators start to dominate and returns diminish. Every format you support adds area inside the most replicated cell on the chip. Eight bits is always enough for inference if quantization is done well. R → Systolic arrays

How the pieces around the array work

12. A systolic array is a reduction chain laid out in space, and a tensor core is a reduction tree. Both compute dot products. The chain uses only neighbor wires but has latency proportional to K. The tree has logarithmic latency but needs fan-in wiring. Real designs mix them: small trees inside a processing element, chains between elements. DO → Reduction trees

13. Crossbar cost grows with the square of the port count, so nobody uses one flat crossbar at scale. You pay in wires, and the die is a 2D plane. Designs use small crossbars inside clusters, then meshes or rings between clusters. EIA → Crossbars and NoC

14. Memory is just another node on the network. Where you attach SRAM and HBM to the fabric determines hop counts, contention and energy. How the network on chip is set up matters as much as how much memory you have. IA → Crossbars and NoC

15. Who decides what lives in SRAM changes the whole machine. If hardware decides, it is a cache. If software decides, it is a scratchpad. A scratchpad removes tag arrays, replacement logic and timing uncertainty, and it moves that complexity into your compiler. For high-performance AI, manual control ends up being the more convenient option. IARJ → Memory

16. Complexity is conserved. You choose where it lives. Groq removed arbiters, caches and replay, and its design is simple enough for a small team to reproduce. The complexity went into the hardest compiler ever written. Warp scheduling puts the same pipelining in hardware at a large area cost. Software pipelining puts it in a library. IAR → Control and feeding

17. Queues buy decoupling, and they do not buy bandwidth. A deep FIFO absorbs a temporary mismatch between producer and consumer. It does nothing for a permanent mismatch. Size queues from latency times bandwidth, because one undersized DMA queue can stall a whole core. RD → Control and feeding

18. Cycle tyranny sneaks up on people. An array consumes vectors every cycle, and whatever drives it must never miss a beat. One real chip project could never reach full array rate because its control core could not keep up. Two-dimensional registers, queues, slower array clocks and DMA-fed arrays all reduce this pressure. R → Control and feeding

19. Non-matmul work is small until it is your bottleneck. Softmax, normalization, quantization and activation functions run on the vector unit. Amdahl's law applies at the worst moment: if the array gets 10× faster and the vector unit does not, the vector unit becomes the chip. Ironwood went from two restricted ALUs per lane to four general ones. J → Vector units

Workloads and systems

20. Prefill and training want compute, decode wants memory, and the difference is arithmetic intensity. A prefill step reuses each byte across thousands of tokens. A naive decode step reuses it once. The same chip therefore has idle arrays during decode and idle memory during prefill. R → Workloads

21. Decode attention is hurt by different things than decode feed-forward. Batch fixes feed-forward because users share weights. Batch does nothing for attention because users do not share keys. Grouped-query attention and speculative decoding fix attention instead, by a combined factor like 64×. R → Workloads

22. Most provisioning answers swing by 10× to 100× depending on software. How much bandwidth, how much HBM and how many chips all depend on how well software uses them. Big HBM and big networks partly exist to protect customers from their own inefficient software. R → Workloads

23. The balance of the TPU line has drifted hard toward compute. Across five generations, peak BF16 per unit of HBM bandwidth rose about 5×. VMEM per unit of compute fell about 13×, and interconnect per unit of compute fell about 20×. My reading is that this works because software got better at reuse and overlap. Each generation asks for more batch. D → Generations

24. Pipelining across layers helps weights but not KV cache. Splitting within layers helps both, and costs network bandwidth. This surprises almost everyone, including the people who sized TPU v2's network. Doubling within-layer parallelism a bit more than doubles per-chip bandwidth. R → Scale-out

25. A router hop wastes at least half your bandwidth, and a torus can waste none, until mixture-of-experts shows up. The classic collectives need only neighbor traffic. MoE traffic is all-to-all, which favors small tori and routed fabrics. This is why topology is still contested between Google's torus and Nvidia's NVLink. RIA → Scale-out

26. At scale, reliability is an architecture feature. Google's optical switches exist mainly so a failed rack does not take down a pod. Ironwood added a spare array row, functional self-test and hardware replay to catch silent errors. Parallelism multiplies failure domains, and only duplication reduces them. JR → Scale-out

How great designers think

27. Stability beats novelty. TPU v2's block diagram still describes Ironwood eight years later. Generations scaled the components and kept the architecture, so compilers and models carried over. Five generations of progress came mostly from more of the same blocks, running faster. J → Generations

28. Six decisions turned out to matter most, in this order. Systolic arrays. Narrow floating point chosen for range. HBM. Custom chip-to-chip links. Software-managed scratchpads with DMA. Vector units for everything else. J → Generations

29. Parametrize everything by array width. Write VECTOR_WIDTH as a constant in hardware and software. You can then test on 2×2 tiles where a human can check each number, fit the design on an FPGA, and change the array size between generations without a rewrite. Your RTL already does this, which is the right instinct. R → Your chip

30. Numbers mean nothing without context, and derived consequences change the answer. Turning off op fusion in a compiler built around fusion measures nothing useful. Every hardware experiment needs the question: how would software change in response? Design-space search beats hill climbing, because savings combine superlinearly and bloat protects bloat. R → Judgement

The one-paragraph version

Start from a workload and a cost metric. Compute its arithmetic intensity at the batch you can afford. That tells you whether you are buying compute, bandwidth or capacity. Choose array width from the smallest K you must run efficiently, and array count from your area and power budget. Choose numerics as narrow as your models tolerate. Size SRAM so tiles reach the machine's ridge point and double-buffer cleanly. Size DMA queues from bandwidth times latency. Give the vector unit enough throughput that softmax and quantization hide behind the array. Pick parallelism before you pick network bandwidth, and pick topology from your real traffic pattern. Then check every number against what software will really do, because software decides how much of all this you needed.

NextThe frame

Foundations

The frame: what you are optimizing

Chip design has more interacting decisions than anyone can hold in their head. This chapter gives you the frame that keeps them organized. Every later chapter hangs off it.

Start from a goal you can measure

A chip is a bet that a certain workload will run at a certain cost. Before any block diagram, you need four things written down.

Decide first Why it controls everything
The workload: model family, sizes, context length, precision Sets matmul shapes, which set array size
The service target: tokens per second per user, first-token time Sets batch ceiling, which sets arithmetic intensity
The cost metric: tokens per dollar, or per watt Tells you what a saved mm² or watt is worth
The software you control Sets how much overprovisioning you must buy

Roune's central tension is between maximizing tokens per dollar and overprovisioning so that customers get something familiar. R His claim is that large HBM, big routed networks and host computers exist partly to protect unsophisticated software. If you control the whole stack, you can buy less hardware. If customers bring arbitrary software, you need margin.

Jouppi's team adds that the metric itself moved. Performance per watt has overtaken performance per total cost of ownership, because electricity for new data centers is now the constraint. J Your metric depends on what is scarce for your customer.

The four-question description of any computer

Irrational Analysis proposes that any machine can be compared on four attributes, however strange it is. IA Use this every time you read about a new chip.

1. Memory hierarchy. Is on-chip SRAM a cache or a scratchpad? What does a miss cost? How many levels are there? What is the ratio of SRAM to DRAM?

2. Memory access and routing. Given a piece of memory and a piece of compute, how does data get between them? Ring, mesh, crossbar, or a mix? Memory is a node on the network, so this matters as much as the memory itself.

3. Compute structure. How fancy is each core (speculation, out-of-order)? How many operands per instruction (SIMD, warps, systolic arrays)? Which data formats?

4. Chip-to-chip structure. All-to-all through switches, a torus, dragonfly? This is often where the real differences hide.

Memory Routing Compute Chip to chip
AMD Genoa-X Caches, large L3, stacked SRAM Nested rings Very fancy, weak on matrices Dual socket, no scale-up fabric
Intel Sapphire Rapids Caches, sliced L3 Mesh Very fancy Up to 8 sockets
Nvidia GB300 Caches plus scratchpad, HBM Mesh inside GPC, crossbar above Medium fancy, warp-32 plus tensor cores 72-way all-to-all over copper
Google Ironwood Scratchpad, HBM Crossbar Medium, big systolic arrays, VLIW 3D torus with optical switches
Groq LPU Scratchpad only, no DRAM Streaming lanes, statically scheduled Simple, 144-wide VLIW, 320-wide SIMD Dragonfly, software-scheduled

Adapted from the summary table in IA.

Think in levels

The encyclopedia makes a point that is easy to forget: its 40 categories are not all at the same level. "A matrix engine contains arithmetic units, gates, and transistors." E A useful stack, from bottom to top:

  1. Devices and wires. Transistors, metal layers, vias. Sets delay, leakage and energy per switch.
  2. Cells. Gates, flip-flops, SRAM bitcells. What your synthesis tool sees.
  3. Datapath blocks. Multipliers, adders, register files, FIFOs.
  4. Engines. Systolic arrays, vector units, DMA engines.
  5. Core. An engine set with its control and local memory.
  6. Die. Cores plus NoC, memory controllers, PHYs.
  7. Package. Dies plus HBM, interposer, power delivery.
  8. System. Boards, links, switches, cooling.
  9. Software and model. Which decides how much of all the above you use.

When someone argues about a chip, ask which level they are arguing at. A claim true at level 3 can be irrelevant at level 8.

The encyclopedia's five questions

For any block you consider adding, the encyclopedia ends with a test that is worth memorizing. E

  • What work does it perform?
  • What supplies its data?
  • What limits its throughput?
  • How much state and routing does it require?
  • Does the target process or IP library support it?

Balance, stated precisely

A balanced chip is one where, on the target workload, no resource is far more idle than the others. Roune lists the things that must be balanced together. R Systolic compute, vector compute, scalar compute, memory bandwidth, memory capacity, network bandwidth, watts and thermals, thermal throttling, and the latencies of various operations.

Three ratios give you most of the picture.

Ratio Formula What it tells you
Ridge point Peak FLOP/s ÷ memory bytes/s The reuse software must achieve per byte
Capacity ratio HBM bytes ÷ peak FLOP/s How much state each unit of compute can hold
Network ratio Link bytes/s ÷ peak FLOP/s How much parallelism you can afford

The whole history of TPUs can be read from these three numbers, which we do in the Generations chapter.

System performance is the only performance

Per-chip numbers can mislead you. A chip half as fast with half the HBM costs the same HBM per unit of work. A network one-eighth the price on a chip one-eighth as fast saves nothing. R Always divide by realized system performance. This is also the force that pushes chips to be large: fixed costs per chip, such as a host, a package and network ports, amortize better over more compute.

Goodput is the system-level version of this idea. A system that spends 10% of its time recovering has a goodput of 0.9× its throughput. Google reports 93% goodput for Gemini 2.5 across multiple pods. J

How to use the rest of this guide

Read Area, clock, power next for the physical budget. Then read Systolic arrays and Matmul shape together, since they are the center of everything. The chapters on reduction trees, crossbars, memory, control and vector units cover what surrounds the array. Workloads and Scale-out cover how software and systems set requirements. Generations shows how real designers moved through all of this. Method turns it into a procedure, and Your chip applies it to your RTL.

Foundations

Area, clock, power

The PDFs mostly assume you already know the physical budget, so much of this chapter is O: standard engineering, with ballpark numbers you should replace using a real PDK. What the PDFs add is how designers use these constraints. Treat every number marked O as a starting estimate. The method matters more than the values.

The three budgets are one budget

Area, clock and power trade against each other through a few equations. You rarely get to choose all three.

  • Throughput = number of MACs × clock × utilization.
  • Power ≈ activity × capacitance × voltage² × clock + leakage.
  • Clock rises with voltage, and falls with logic depth and wire length.
  • Area sets how many MACs and how much SRAM you can have, and how much leakage you carry.

Because you can reach the same throughput with many slow MACs or few fast ones, the real question is always which budget binds first.

Area

The hard ceiling

A single exposure on a lithography tool covers about 26 × 33 mm, or roughly 858 mm². O No monolithic die can be larger, apart from wafer-scale tricks like Cerebras. R Designs that want more use several dies in a package. Ironwood uses two compute dies, and Blackwell Ultra pairs two dies with a 10 TB/s link. JIA

Yield makes big dies expensive

With a simple Poisson model, the fraction of good dies is exp(−area × defect_density). At a defect density of 0.1 per cm²:

Die area Good dies D
200 mm² 82%
400 mm² 67%
600 mm² 55%
800 mm² 45%

The usual answer is redundancy. Memory has spare rows and columns. GPUs ship with some cores disabled. Ironwood applied the memory idea to compute by adding a redundant row in the MXU. J A regular array is ideal for this, since one spare row can cover a defect anywhere in the array.

Where area goes

Block How it scales Rough size O
8-bit MAC with registers Shrinks with logic density About 100–150 µm² at 5 nm
16-bit float MAC, FP32 accumulate About 5× an int8 MAC About 500–800 µm² at 5 nm
SRAM macro Shrinks slowly About 0.3–0.4 mm² per MiB at 5 nm
HBM PHY Barely shrinks, needs die edge About 15 mm² per stack
High-speed SerDes Barely shrinks, needs die edge About 0.3–0.5 mm² per lane

Calibration point: TPU v1 spent about 24% of a 331 mm² die at 28 nm on 65,536 int8 MACs, about 1,200 µm² per MAC. O Arrays are a smaller share of real dies than people expect. Vector units, NoC, control and I/O add up quickly, so the lab budgets those at 50% of array area plus a fixed amount. Even so, expect real dies to come out larger than the lab shows.

SRAM stopped scaling

Jouppi states it plainly: SRAM density grew more slowly than logic density, so VMEM only quadrupled from 32 to 128 MiB in eight years despite a much larger die. J This one fact drives a lot of current design. It is why AMD stacks SRAM dies on its CPUs, why hybrid bonding is attractive for Groq-style designs, and why SRAM chiplets on older nodes make economic sense. IA

AMD's lesson is instructive. It stacks extra cache only on top of existing SRAM and puts blank structural silicon over the CPU cores, because stacking on hot compute is hard. IA

Beachfront: the budget people forget

HBM PHYs and SerDes must sit at the die edge. Edge length grows with the square root of area, while compute grows with area. So as dies get bigger, each mm² of compute has less edge available for I/O. The area question becomes a perimeter question. This is one reason multi-die packages exist: two dies have more total edge than one die of the same total area.

Ironwood's eight HBM stacks sit on either side of its two compute dies, with interconnect SerDes on a separate chiplet. JIA

Clock

What sets the period

period = clock-to-q + logic delay + setup + skew + jitter

Everything except logic delay is overhead. If overhead is about 80 ps O, a 500 ps period gives you 420 ps of useful work. Halve the period and useful work falls to 170 ps, so you need more than twice the pipeline stages, with more flip-flops and more power. That is why clock frequency has diminishing returns.

Wires are the real limit

A repeated wire on mid-level metal takes on the order of 100 ps per mm. O Crossing a 20 mm die therefore takes about 2 ns. At 2 GHz that is four cycles, before you do any logic. Three consequences follow.

  • Local wiring wins. A systolic array only talks to its neighbors, so its critical path does not grow with array size. This is its deepest physical advantage.
  • Global signals must be pipelined. Anything broadcast to every processing element, like enable or clear_acc, cannot reach 65,536 cells in one cycle.
  • Big cores have a limit. TPUs use two large TensorCores because that balanced longer wire latencies in one huge core against exposing many tiny cores that software must lash together. J

Should the array run fast?

Early TPUs ran arrays at lower clocks so that the scalar and vector side could keep up. R Look at the implied clocks from Jouppi's Table 1 D:

Generation Implied clock
TPU v2 0.70 GHz
TPU v3 0.94 GHz
TPU v4 1.05 GHz
TPU v5p 1.75 GHz
Ironwood About 2.2 GHz, see the audit chapter

From v2 to Ironwood, BF16 peak rose 50×. About 3× came from clock, and the rest came from more MACs. Clock was never the main lever.

Reasons to run an array slower:

  • Control and feeding logic have more slack.
  • Lower voltage cuts energy per operation.
  • Hotspots shrink.

Reasons to run it faster:

  • Fewer MACs for the same throughput, saving area and leakage.
  • Lower latency per tile.

Power

The equation to memorize

P_dynamic = α · C · V² · f

α is the fraction of nodes switching per cycle, C is total switched capacitance, V is the supply voltage and f is the clock. Two things stand out. Voltage is squared. And α depends on your data, which is why worst-case power is so much higher than typical power.

Leakage power flows even when nothing switches, and grows with temperature. Roune notes that a hotter chip draws more power, causing more heat. R

Energy per operation: the numbers that shape architecture

Horowitz's 45 nm numbers are the classic reference. O Absolute values have improved since, but ratios have held up reasonably well.

Operation Energy at 45 nm
8-bit add 0.03 pJ
8-bit multiply 0.2 pJ
32-bit float multiply 3.7 pJ
32-bit read, 8 KB SRAM 10 pJ
32-bit read, 1 MB SRAM About 100 pJ
32-bit read, DRAM About 640–1300 pJ

Read that table as an architect would. A DRAM read costs thousands of times more than an 8-bit multiply. Reading a value from a large SRAM costs far more than computing with it. So every byte you fetch must be used many times. A systolic array earns its efficiency because a value fetched once is used across a whole row or column of MACs, moving only between neighbors. Systolic arrays produce far less heat per operation than other structures. R

Modern ballparks for planning O:

Action Energy
int8 MAC with local registers About 0.2 pJ
BF16 MAC with FP32 accumulate About 0.4–0.6 pJ
SRAM read per byte About 1–3 pJ
HBM read per byte About 30 pJ
Chip-to-chip copper per byte About 15–40 pJ

The wide-and-slow trade

Because voltage is squared, you can trade area for energy. Take a teaching curve where frequency follows the alpha-power law, with threshold 0.3 V at a nominal 0.75 V. Dropping to 75% of the clock allows about 0.61 V, cutting dynamic energy per operation to about 65%. D You need 1.33× the MACs for the same throughput.

This is Roune's point about larger clocked-down arrays, and it is what Etched's low-voltage inference pitch relies on. RF It pays off when power is the binding limit and area is available. It stops paying when leakage from the extra area, or the cost of that area, outweighs the saving.

Heat is about density

Average power density for a 1 kW chip on 800 mm² is 1.25 W/mm². D Arrays can run several times hotter than that, since they pack so much computation into a small area. The TPU v3 story shows what happens if you get this wrong. R

  • The team underestimated array heat, and it showed up when silicon arrived.
  • The hardware throttle measured temperature after the fact, which was too slow for spikes inside the array.
  • The fix was a compiler static analysis, validated against an empirical heat model, that refused to emit instruction patterns that could overheat the array.
  • That allowed a 25% higher clock. Roune called it compiler throttling and later wished he had called it Turbo Mode.

The lessons are general.

You cannot provision for the worst case. Worst-case data and instruction patterns draw far more power than anything useful does. Every high-performance chip therefore throttles. Without it, a malicious cloud tenant could destroy hardware. R

Throttle on current, not only temperature. Measuring electrical power reacts faster than temperature sensors do. R

Peak and sustained are different numbers. A chip that throttles quickly can advertise a clock it cannot hold. Compare long-running benchmarks instead. R

Placement is a thermal tool. Spread arrays apart, or interleave them with cooler logic. R

Delivering the current

A 1 kW chip at 0.75 V draws 1,333 amps. D Resistance in the power network turns directly into lost voltage, and every millivolt of droop eats timing margin. When a large array starts all at once, current jumps and the supply sags. Two responses appear in the sources: more decoupling and better delivery paths such as vertical power and backside power JE, and droop detectors that throttle before a timing failure E.

A useful detail of systolic arrays: their diagonal wavefront ramps activity up gradually, which softens that current step compared with a design where everything starts on the same cycle. O

Power-saving structures

Each saves something different, and each has a cost in the encyclopedia's terms. E

Technique What it saves What it costs
Clock gating Clock tree and flop switching in idle logic Enable timing, a gating cell
Operand isolation, zero gating Datapath toggling on zero operands A small amount of control
Power gating Leakage in sleeping blocks Wake latency, state loss unless retained
DVFS Energy at lower demand Regulators, characterization
Multiple Vt cells Leakage on paths with slack Library and sign-off complexity

Reasoning procedure

  1. Compute required MACs from throughput ÷ (clock × target utilization).
  2. Convert MACs to area and power using your node's numbers.
  3. Add SRAM area for tiles, PHY area for bandwidth and control overhead.
  4. Check perimeter against PHY and SerDes needs.
  5. Check total watts against cooling, and peak density against the array.
  6. If power binds, go wider and slower. If area binds, go narrower and faster, or use more dies.
  7. Compute yield and decide what needs redundancy.

The lab above lets you do this interactively. Its constants are defaults you can replace, and they are not measurements of any product.

The compute core

Systolic arrays

"It's all systolic arrays." R This is the engine of the chip. This chapter covers how one works, how to size it, and every knob you can tune.

A note on sources. Roune states that his document is not an explanation of systolic arrays, and he skips skew on purpose. R So your PDFs give the reasons and the big decisions, while most of the beat-level mechanics here are O, drawn from the published designs listed at the end, or D, checked with a beat-by-beat simulator in deep_dive/model/sim_array.js.

Why matmul wins

A matrix multiply has more arithmetic than data. Multiplying two N×N matrices takes about 2N³ operations on 3N² numbers, so each number can be reused about N times. A systolic array physically implements this reuse. Each value enters at the edge once, then passes between neighbors, doing a multiply at every stop. Only the edge touches memory.

Systolic arrays were invented in 1978. They became important because AI suddenly created demand for them. R They are the first of the six features Jouppi ranks as most important in training accelerators. J

Anatomy of a processing element

Your pe.sv is a good reference. Each PE holds:

  • A multiplier: 8×8 gives a 16-bit product.
  • An adder and accumulator: 32 bits in your design.
  • Pipeline registers that pass operands to neighbors.

The cost breakdown surprises people. In an 8-bit output-stationary PE you have 8 + 8 + 32 = 48 flip-flops for one multiply. A flip-flop costs several gates, so storage and clocking are a large share of the PE. This drives the grouped PE idea in the next chapter.

The three dataflows

What stays still decides what moves. Name the dataflow before you use any formula, because array dimensions mean different things in each. R

Dataflow Stationary Moving Good for Costs
Output-stationary Accumulators A rows, B columns Long K, narrow data wires Need a readout path, no weight reuse across tiles
Weight-stationary Weights Activations, partial sums Many rows per weight tile Wide partial sums move every hop, weight load time
Input-stationary Activations Weights, partial sums Rarely the best for LLMs Same as weight-stationary, mirrored

TPUs are weight-stationary. Your sys_array.sv is output-stationary. Neither is universally right.

Wire traffic comparison for int8. An output-stationary PE moves 8 + 8 = 16 bits per cycle between neighbors. A weight-stationary PE moves 8 activation bits and 32 partial-sum bits, for 40 bits, once the weights are loaded. D Output-stationary is cheaper to run in steady state. Weight-stationary avoids a readout network and pairs naturally with accumulators outside the array.

What a beat is

A beat is one tick of the array's clock. On every beat, each value moves one hop to its neighbor, and each PE does its work on whatever just arrived. The word systolic comes from the heartbeat for this reason: the whole array pumps together.

Everything in this chapter comes down to three questions about a beat:

  • How many beats until every PE has work? That is fill.
  • How many beats until the last PE has finished? That is drain.
  • How much work does one PE do in one beat? That is packing.

The timing that matters

For an output-stationary R×C array computing an R×C tile with reduction depth K, operands are skewed so element k reaches PE(r,c) at beat k + r + c.

tile cycles = K + R + C − 2

This is exactly TOTAL_CYCLES in your tile_engine.sv. Utilization for one isolated tile is K / (K + R + C − 2).

Watch a small one run

Take a 3×3 array with K = 4. PE(r,c) works during beats r+c through r+c+3.

Beat PEs working Out of 9 What is happening
0 1 11% Only the corner has data
1 3 33% Filling
2 6 67% Filling
3 8 89% Near the peak, and the corner is on its last value
4 8 89% The corner has finished
5 6 67% Draining
6 3 33% Draining
7 1 11% Only the far corner is left

The total is 8 beats, which is 4 + 3 + 3 − 2. The array did 36 MACs in 72 slots, so it ran at 50%. With K this short, all nine PEs are never busy at once.

Fill and drain are one tax. Each PE works for exactly K beats, and sits idle for the other R+C−2. A PE near the first corner idles at the end, one near the far corner idles at the start, and one in the middle does some of each. So the array does not pay for fill and then again for drain. It pays R+C−2 once, split between the two ends. D

Weight-stationary timing

The same diagonal appears, with three differences. Time for T tiles of M activation rows each, once weights are in place: D

beats = T × M + R + C − 2

  • Weights must first shift in, one row per beat, so R beats per tile. TPU v1 quotes this: 256 cycles to shift a tile in. O
  • Partial sums now travel down the column, so the last result leaves the bottom row R−1 beats after its activation entered. This is drain, and it is real wire traffic rather than idle time.
  • The stream length is M, not K. So at decode, with M = 1, there is almost no stream to hide anything behind. This is why the rows-needed equation in Matmul shape exists.

Simulators often count one more thing. SCALE-Sim's standard estimate is 2R + C + T − 2, which is this chapter's formula plus R beats to carry results out. O Both are right. They stop the clock at different moments, so check which one a paper is using.

What isolated tiles cost

Array K=16 K=64 K=256 K=4096
8×8 53% 82% 95% 100%
32×32 20% 50% 80% 98%
128×128 6% 20% 50% 94%
256×256 3% 11% 33% 89%

Those are the numbers for isolated tiles. D They look terrible for big arrays with short K, and most of the next section is about not paying them.

Rule of thumb. Fraction lost = (R+C−2) ÷ (stream + R+C−2). For about 90% utilization, the stream must be roughly ten times R+C. D

Cutting fill and drain

There are only four strategies. You can pay the tax less often, make the tax smaller, put other work in the gap, or make the idle beats cheap.

Trick Fill on 256×256 What it costs Source
Nothing 510 per tile Nothing D
Pay less often: run tiles back to back 510 once per stream Shadow registers, tags that travel with data RO
Pay less often: order loops for long streams 510 once per longer stream More accumulators or more SRAM D
Shrink: four 128×128 arrays 254 Four sets of control, twice the edge bandwidth RD
Shrink: 2×2 MACs per register stage 254 Longer wires, fanout of 2, lower top clock OD
Shrink: broadcast one operand 255 Long buffered wire across every row OD
Shrink: broadcast both operands 0 No longer really systolic, wires limit the clock OD
Shrink: feed from the diagonal 255 Feed wires into the array interior O
Shrink: split columns with an adder tree (WS drain) R÷S + log₂S S output taps per column, tree area OD
Fill the gap: independent work Unchanged, but used A scheduler, a second stream RD
Make it cheap: clock-gate idle PEs Unchanged in time One gating cell, enable timing E

Pay less often: run tiles back to back

This is the big one, and it comes first because nothing else gets close. Roune describes the idea directly: feed the next B while processing the current A and outputting the prior C, so the left, top and right edges are all busy on every cycle. R

Start tile 2 one beat behind tile 1, like cars in a convoy. Each PE finishes its last value of tile 1 and gets its first value of tile 2 on the very next beat. The diagonal band never goes away, and the ramp is paid once for the whole stream.

T back-to-back tiles = T × K + R + C − 2

For K = 256, here is what that buys. D

Tiles in a row 128×128 256×256
1 50% 33%
4 80% 67%
16 94% 89%
64 99% 97%

This needs real hardware changes, covered in What overlap actually needs below.

What overlap cannot do. It only works when the next tile does not depend on this one. Tiles in one matmul are independent. The next layer is not, because it needs this layer's last output before it can finish, and in a Transformer a LayerNorm or softmax usually sits between them. So you pay the ramp at least once per dependent stage, and this is the number to count at batch 1. D

Pay less often: choose a long stream

The stream is whatever you loop over while the same thing stays in place. For output-stationary, keep the accumulators and walk all of K before you read out. Your init_acc=0 already allows this: tiles that continue the same sum need no readout between them. For weight-stationary, hold weights while as many rows as possible pass through. D

Shrink: put more MACs behind each register

Fill is counted in hops. If a value crosses two PEs per beat, there are half as many hops. Gemmini exposes this as a generator setting: its array is a mesh of tiles, with pure combinational logic inside a tile and pipeline registers between tiles. O This is the packing section's Tm and Tn, seen from the timing side.

Shrink: broadcast instead of hop

A row can receive one operand on a wire that reaches all its PEs in the same beat. Then a PE's start time depends only on its row, and fill falls from R+C−2 to R−1. Broadcast both operands, and fill is zero.

This gives up the thing that makes an array systolic. A hop is short wire and tiny fanout, whatever the array size. A broadcast's delay grows with length, at the order of 100 ps per mm from Area, clock, power. O So broadcast is fine over a short span and hopeless across a big one. A 64-column int8 row is under 1 mm at 5 nm, on the rough cell sizes in that chapter. A 256-wide array is about 3 mm, which uses most of a 500 ps clock at 2 GHz before fanout or logic. D

Treat it as a dial, not a switch: broadcast within a group of PEs, and hop between groups.

Shrink: feed from the diagonal

Axon injects operands at the PEs on the main diagonal, and sends them outward in both directions. A row's operand starts at PE(r,r) and a column's starts at PE(c,c), so they meet at PE(r,c) at beat |r−c|. Both arrive together with no skew at all, and fill falls to max(R,C)−1, half of what a square array normally pays. O

The paper reports up to 2× runtime on shapes where fill dominates, and about 0.2% area overhead at 16×16 in a 7 nm library. Its average gain at 256×256 is 1.76×. O It was implemented for output-stationary. Weight-stationary needs extra muxes. Treat these as one paper's results, not as established practice.

Shrink: end the column chain early (weight-stationary)

A 256-long chain takes 256 beats to drain. Cut it into S segments, then add the S partial sums at the bottom with a small tree. Drain becomes R÷S + log₂S beats. With S = 4 that is 66, not 256. D The extreme version is a full adder tree per column. The DiP paper notes that the Meissa design did this and that large trees hurt scaling, through wiring congestion and deep pipelines. O Reduction trees covers the trade.

Fill the gap with other work

If a gap is unavoidable, use it.

  • Block-diagonal packing. Two independent small matmuls can occupy the upper-left and lower-right of the array at once, with no hardware feature. R
  • Two arrays, staggered. While one array is at a dependency stall, the other runs a different stream. D
  • Overlap attention with feed-forward. Roune notes this needs deeper pipelines or a model change that runs them in parallel. R
  • A second request. Two independent users can alternate, so one's stage boundary hides behind the other's work. At batch 1 you do not have this option. D

Make it cheap

Clock gating does not give back a single beat, but it means idle PEs burn little dynamic power. E Time and energy are separate budgets here: at batch 1 you may accept the beats and care only about the battery.

What overlap actually needs

Your tile_engine.sv runs IDLE → RUN → DONE, one tile at a time. Three things stop you from just feeding tiles back to back.

1. Clear must travel with the data. Your clear_acc fires at one moment for every PE. That is safe today only because the array is empty when it fires. With overlap, PE(0,0) starts tile 2 while PE(7,7) is still on tile 1, so a global clear would wipe a running sum. The fix is one extra bit that rides beside the first operand, so each PE clears on the beat tile 2 reaches it. TPU v1 describes the same idea for weights: they take effect "with the advancing wave". O

Tag Rides with Tells a PE to
first First K element Start a new sum rather than add
last Final K element Hand the sum to the shadow register
flip First row of a tile (WS) Switch to the preloaded weights
valid Every operand Hold still, since this slot is a bubble

2. The finished sum needs somewhere to go. On the very next beat, the accumulator is needed for tile 2. So each PE holds a second register, called a shadow. Gemmini's PE works this way: two registers, c1 and c2, with a travelling propagate bit picking which one accumulates and which one is read out. In weight-stationary mode the same two registers hold active and next weights. O

This is the price of overlap: 32 more flops per PE, taking an int8 PE from 48 to 80 flops. Packing K, below, shrinks this cost a lot.

3. Results must leave as fast as they arrive. Each column shifts one value per beat, so a tile takes R beats to leave, while the next tile takes K beats to finish. D

tile time = max(K, R)

Our beat simulator confirms the edge exactly: K = R runs with no collisions, and K = R−1 overwrites results. There is a catch. A plain shift-enable for the whole column is not enough, because the next tile's first results land while the old ones are leaving, and they would get dragged along. It takes one tag bit per slot, so that only the old tile moves. D

The weight-stationary version is the same rule in another costume. New weights follow one beat behind the flip wave, deepest row first, so they need R beats: M ≥ R, which is the rows-needed equation at ρ = 1. The simulator confirms this as well: M = R works, and M = R−1 swaps too early. D

TPU v1 shows what a full design looks like: one 64 KiB weight tile active, one for double-buffering to hide the 256 shift cycles, and a Weight FIFO four tiles deep behind them. O

More than one element per beat

So far each PE does one MAC per beat. A PE can do more, and this is one of the most useful knobs you have, because it changes the array's shape without changing how many MACs you pay for.

Call a PE doing several MACs a cell. A cell has three packing factors, one for each matmul dimension:

  • Tk: reduction elements per beat. This is the grouped PE from Reduction trees, where it is called G.
  • Tm: output rows per cell.
  • Tn: output columns per cell.

For an array of Rc × Cc cells, these formulas hold. The simulator checks them for several cell shapes, with real values. D

Quantity Formula
MACs Rc × Cc × Tm × Tn × Tk
Output tile (Rc × Tm) × (Cc × Tn)
Beats per tile ⌈K ÷ Tk⌉ + Rc + Cc − 2
Operands in per beat (Rc × Tm + Cc × Tn) × Tk
Flops per MAC, int8 8(Tm + Tn) ÷ (Tm × Tn) + 32 ÷ Tk

The last formula matches 16 + 32/G when Tm = Tn = 1. The shadow register adds another 32 ÷ Tk.

Packing K: a small dot product per beat

The cell takes Tk values of A and Tk values of B, multiplies them pairwise, and sums them with a small tree into one accumulator.

For Tk = 4, one beat does acc += a0·b0 + a1·b1 + a2·b2 + a3·b3.

  • Good: K takes Tk× fewer beats. One accumulator serves Tk multipliers, so accumulators, shadows, and readout traffic all shrink by Tk.
  • Bad: The tree sits in the critical path, at log₂Tk adder levels. Operand wires get Tk× wider. Reuse falls, because the array is smaller for the same MACs.
  • Watch out: K rounds up to a multiple of Tk. K = 3 on Tk = 4 wastes a quarter of the multipliers.
  • Watch out: Isolated-tile utilization can get worse, because K shrinks by Tk while fill only shrinks by about √Tk. Packing K helps latency, not the utilization of short tiles.
  • Watch out: The readout rule becomes K ÷ Tk ≥ R.

Nvidia's tensor cores sit far toward this end, which is why they can act as systolic arrays at chip level, as Roune treats them, while differing at circuit level. RO

Packing M and N: a small outer product per beat

The cell takes Tm values of A and Tn values of B and does every pairing, into Tm × Tn accumulators. A 2×2 cell does four MACs from four operands, where four separate PEs would need eight operand registers.

  • Good: Fill halves, with the same output tile and the same edge traffic. Fewer operand flops.
  • Bad: Each operand drives Tm or Tn multipliers in the same beat, and has to cross a wider cell. The cost is wire delay and fanout, not logic depth.
  • Unchanged: Accumulators stay at one per MAC.

This is the Gemmini tile from earlier. Taken to its limit, one giant cell has no hops at all: you have an outer-product engine, the structure behind Arm's SME that a reader raises with Roune. His answer is that systolic arrays remain the most area- and power-efficient choice for dedicated AI. R

Packing bits: several narrow numbers in one wide lane

A multiplier can often split. An 8×8 multiplier is built from partial products, and it holds four 4×4 multipliers inside it, since (16·a₁ + a₀)(16·b₁ + b₀) has four terms. The same 8-bit wires carry two 4-bit values each. Gate the carries between the pieces, and one PE does more narrow MACs per beat. O

The reverse also works, and TPU v1 did it: the matrix unit ran at half speed with one 16-bit operand, and quarter speed with two, building wide products out of 8-bit multipliers over several beats. O

Example Packing Source
TPU v1 16-bit operands take 2 or 4 passes on 8-bit hardware O
Ironwood Described as four 256×256 BF16 or four 512×512 FP8 arrays J
RTX Blackwell FP4 at double the FP8 rate O

Read the Ironwood line with care. A 512 side implies four FP8 MACs per BF16 cell, but the published peak is only 2× BF16. Source audit covers this mismatch, so the paper does not settle the real packing factor. JD

Roune's packing notes are the software side of this. Narrow formats need several rows packed into one vector register, so that each register stays full, which forces row counts to be a multiple of that factor. R

Doing fewer multiplies

Two more tricks change the arithmetic itself. They are niche, but they show the design space is wider than it looks.

  • Fast inner product. Winograd's 1968 identity gets two products from one multiply, using cheap pre-additions: (a₀ + b₁)(a₁ + b₀) contains a₀b₀ + a₁b₁, plus correction terms that depend on only one matrix. Pogue and Nicolici's FFIP puts this into systolic arrays for about half the multipliers at fixed-point precision. O
  • Shared-multiplier packing. Place two weights in a wide multiplier with a gap between them, and one multiply by a shared activation gives both products. FPGA designs use this with wide DSP multipliers. O

Same 64 MACs, six ways

All of these are 64 MACs, at K = 64, 16 tiles. D

Array × cell Output tile Fill Beats per tile Isolated Back to back Operands per beat Flops per MAC, with shadow
8×8, plain 8×8 14 64 82% 98.7% 16 80
4×4 of 2×2×1 8×8 6 64 91% 99.4% 16 72
4×4 of 1×1×4 4×4 6 16 73% 97.7% 32 32
2×2 of 2×2×4 4×4 2 16 89% 99.2% 32 24
1×16 of 1×1×4 1×16 15 16 52% 94.5% 68 32
1×64, plain 1×64 63 64 50% 94.2% 65 80

Flops are the pipeline and accumulator registers only. Fill here assumes hops, so a row with a broadcast operand has zero fill.

Read down the columns. Packing M and N (row 2) is close to free, if wires allow it. Packing K (row 3) cuts flops per MAC by more than half, and pays for it with twice the operand traffic. Combining both (row 4) has the shortest fill and fewest flops, and pays with the widest cell. The two rows at the bottom pay more edge traffic because they have no reuse in one direction. That is the price of M = 1, not a design flaw.

Choosing what to pack

If this is your situation Do this
M is small Do not pack Tm. Pack Tk, or use a row
K is short or odd Keep Tk small, since rounding wastes MACs
Fill hurts and wires are short Pack Tm and Tn
Flops or clock power dominate Pack Tk, since one accumulator serves several MACs
SRAM bandwidth binds Keep the array large and square, and avoid Tk
Clock is the priority Keep cells small, with one MAC per register
You need overlap but shadows cost too much Pack Tk, which divides shadow cost by Tk

Skew: the hidden triangle

Skew means row r starts r beats late, so that operands meet at the right PE on the right beat. Roune skips it, saying it is not relevant to his point. R It matters if you build one.

Row r needs r delay stages, so one edge needs R(R−1)/2 registers. D

Side Delay stages per edge Bits for int8 in on two edges Bits for 32-bit deskew out
8 28 448 896
128 8,128 130,048 260,096
256 32,640 522,240 1,044,480

The output column only applies to weight-stationary arrays whose consumer needs aligned rows. Your options:

Option How it works Cost
Triangle of flops or FIFOs The textbook edge The table above
Staggered SRAM addresses Each row's bank reads with its own offset No delay registers, needs a bank per row
Index logic Your k_idx = clock_count − row A mux per row that grows with K
Let the consumer stay skewed Downstream lanes also run a beat apart Skew must be planned chip-wide
Diagonal feed Axon needs no skew Feed wires into the interior O
Permuted weights DiP moves inputs diagonally and permutes the weights, removing the FIFOs New dataflow, one paper's result O

DiP reports up to 1.49× throughput and up to 2.02× energy efficiency per area over its weight-stationary baseline in a 22 nm flow. O Again, that is one paper against its own baseline.

Reading results out

Fill gets the attention, but readout is often the real problem. An R×C tile of 32-bit sums is a lot of data.

Method Beats to empty Wires Good for
Parallel bus, like your ACC 1 R × C × 32 Tiny arrays only
Column shift, array waits R, exposed C × 32 Simple small designs
Column shift with shadow R, hidden if K ≥ R C × 32 Output-stationary at scale
Sums flow out the bottom (WS) Hidden in the stream C × 32 TPUs, with accumulators outside
Requantize at the edge As above, narrower memory C × 32, then C × 8 Inference

TPU v1 used the fourth: 4 MiB of accumulators below the array, as 4,096 entries of 256 × 32 bits. Google sized it from the roofline knee of about 1,350 operations per byte, rounded up to 2,048, and doubled for double-buffering. O Notice the method: a memory sized from a bandwidth ratio, not from a guess.

Bubbles and stalls

A global stall has the same problem as a global clear: no signal reaches every PE in one beat. So large arrays do not freeze. They let bubbles flow. A valid bit rides with each operand, and a PE simply holds its registers when the bit is low. Gemmini's PE does this. O

To keep bubbles rare, you need the feed to be reliable. TPU v1's array stalls if activations or weights are not ready, and it stages weights through that four-deep FIFO to reduce the chance. O

Feeding the array on every beat is what Roune calls cycle tyranny, and he knows of a chip that could never reach full utilization because its controlling core could not keep up. R His remedies are 8×128 two-dimensional registers, hardware queues, unrolled loops, slower array clocks, and DMAs that stream straight into the array. R Control and feeding covers them. Packing interacts with this directly: Tk multiplies the operands needed per beat, while the array issues the same MACs in fewer beats.

Repair and test

A regular array makes a defect cheap to repair. Ironwood added a redundant row to the MXU, and it runs a Functional Built-In Self-Test engine inside it, to catch bad chips in manufacturing and in the field. J To skip a dead row, operands and partial sums need a bypass mux around each row. O A longer path through that mux lands on the hop you most want to keep short, so plan for it from the start.

One PE, two dataflows

You do not have to choose forever. Gemmini can be built with output-stationary, weight-stationary, or both, picked at runtime. In "both" mode, the two registers in each PE serve as double-buffered accumulators in one mode, and as active and next weights in the other. O The price is muxes in the most replicated cell in the chip, plus an accumulator memory outside the array for weight-stationary mode.

Your chip

Your workload has 13 dependent stages per token: six in each of two layers, plus the LM head. D Overlap cannot hide those boundaries, so the ramp is paid 13 times per token, and batch 1 gives you no second stream to fill it. These estimates come from the model, not from your RTL.

64-MAC design Work beats per token Ramp, 13 stages Total Accumulators
1×64 row, operand hops 2,048 819 2,867 64
1×64 row, operand broadcast 2,048 0 2,048 64
1×16 of Tk=4, operand hops 1,920 195 2,115 16
1×16 of Tk=4, operand broadcast 1,920 0 1,920 16

Three points follow. Broadcasting x removes a 40% slowdown, and at this size the wire is short, so that is a clear win. D The ROWS=1, COLS=64 setting of your current RTL is the first row of this table.

The Tk=4 row is worth a look. It is 6% faster, because attention's narrow N of 32 wastes half of a 64-wide row. It also has a quarter of the accumulators, which is 1,536 fewer flops at 32 bits, and it needs only 16 readout lanes. The price is a two-level adder tree in the PE and a 4-byte x bus. At your clock that tree is probably affordable, but only synthesis can confirm it. Every K in your model is a multiple of 4, apart from attention values at odd context lengths, where the last group is partly empty.

Weight traffic stays at 64 bytes per beat in all four rows. That is the real limit, and no packing changes it at M = 1.

Why bigger is better

Compare one 2N×2N array with four N×N arrays. They do the same math per cycle. The large one needs one control stream rather than four, and its operand vectors are only twice as wide, rather than four times the total. R

Going from N to 2N Change
Math per cycle 4×
Edge bandwidth needed 2×
Scalar work per unit of math ÷4
Vector work per unit of math ÷2
Bytes moved per MAC ÷2

From a 4×4 array to a 128×128 array is five doublings, so 1024× less scalar work and 32× less vector work. With TPU's 8×128 registers the scalar saving reaches 8192×. R Roune attributes much of the TPU team's ability to keep up with Nvidia to this one fact.

Bigger arrays also make the whole chip easier to build. Arrays and caches are simple and keep getting more area. The complex CPU-like logic shrinks as a fraction of the die, so it needs less optimization. R

Why not build it infinitely large

Four forces limit array size. R

1. Shape mismatch. An N×N array cannot efficiently do a smaller matmul. This is the main force, covered in the next chapter.

2. Batch and latency. Large arrays need more rows per weight tile, which means larger batches, more KV cache and more token latency.

3. The rest of the chip. Scalar, vector and memory blocks need space. TPU v1 was nearly one big array, but it needed an external CPU to drive it, so that area moved to another chip you still had to buy.

4. Heat density. Concentrated computing concentrates heat, though Roune says this can be managed and should not limit size.

Roune's reading is that attention is what holds array size down. Without it, we might have 1024×1024 arrays today.

Replication

Once an array hits its size limit, you add more of them. Replication multiplies all costs and benefits, with small savings from sharing. R Ironwood's move from 128² arrays to 256² arrays fits this logic. My reading is that feed-forward efficiency outweighed attention utilization for a workload that was 74% Transformer by 2026. JD

Decomposable arrays split into smaller ones on demand, as Etched and MatX describe. RF The catch: to run in small mode you must already have paid for the on-chip bandwidth and control that small mode needs, so you lose the area saving of a large array. You can still gain some power. R

Heterogeneous arrays are Roune's suggestion: one big array for feed-forward and several small ones for attention, identical except for VECTOR_WIDTH. Whatever ratio you pick is better than the 100% to one side that uniform designs give you. R

Numerics: making each cell cheap

Multiplier area grows roughly with the product of operand widths, so going narrower has compounding benefits: less multiplier area, less energy, half the memory traffic, half the capacity.

Format Bits (sign, exponent, mantissa) Key property
FP32 1, 8, 23 Original baseline, expensive
FP16 1, 5, 10 Needs loss scaling for training
BF16 1, 8, 7 FP32 range, drop-in for training, cheaper than FP16
FP8 E4M3 1, 4, 3 Forward pass
FP8 E5M2 1, 5, 2 More range, used for gradients
Int8 8-bit integer Simplest hardware, enough for inference
FP4 1, 2, 1 Barely usable, weights easier than activations
MXFP4 and NVFP4 4 bits plus shared scale About 4.25 bits, for models that nearly work in 4

The key design rules:

  • Multiply narrow, accumulate wide. Multiplies tolerate low precision. Sums do not. BF16 multiplies accumulate in FP32. J
  • Range beats precision. BF16 was the first format to give the exponent more bits than the fraction, and later narrow formats followed that lead. J
  • Diminishing returns below 8 bits. Accumulators stop shrinking, and at FP4 the sum may cost more than the product. An FP4 product fits exactly in int8 fixed point, so integer summation could be cheaper. R
  • Bandwidth gains do not diminish. FP4 still halves memory traffic even when the compute saving tails off. R
  • Every format costs area in the most replicated cell. Nvidia's many formats must carry a real price. Google avoids paying for FP16. R
  • Array numerics can differ from vector numerics. You can have int8 arrays and FP32 vectors, since the vector unit is small. R

How low can you go? Eight bits is always enough for inference if quantization is done right. Five bits is usually enough. Four is sometimes enough. R TPU v1 was pure int8 and suffered in adoption because in 2015 few people knew how to quantize. That barrier has gone, so an int8-only inference chip is a real contender. R

Sparsity

Unstructured sparsity does not fit a regular array. Structured A:B sparsity does. In 2:4 sparsity, each group of 4 holds at most 2 non-zeros. Nvidia has supported it since Ampere for about 2× throughput at modest area, with metadata of 3 bits per 4 entries. R

Roune proposes going further with 1:2 sparsity and a 7-bit integer: an 8-bit format with one position bit and seven value bits. It is simple and SIMD-friendly, but unproven.

Be careful with this one. Roune is an advocate, and the same document records a practitioner's objection that accuracy drops are too large and that almost nobody uses 2:4 at scale. R Sparsity also applies mainly to weights. It does not speed up attention's activation-times-activation matmuls, and it does nothing for KV cache. Treat it as a bet that depends on your model team.

Knob Raise it to Pay with Watch for

The papers behind the O items in this chapter. These sit outside your four PDFs. I read the relevant passages directly, apart from FFIP, where I read only the abstract and introduction.

The compute core

Matmul shape

This chapter answers the question you asked directly: how do designers reason about matmul shape? It is the most important chapter in the guide.

Naming the three dimensions

A matrix multiply has three dimensions. This guide uses standard GEMM names throughout.

C[M × N] = A[M × K] · B[K × N]

  • M: rows of activations. Tokens times batch.
  • K: the reduction depth. How many products sum into one output.
  • N: output features. Columns of the weight matrix.

Roune uses N for rows and M for columns, so swap them when you read his document. His "N rows of LHS" is our M.

Picture the computation as a box of size M × N × K. Each small cube inside is one multiply-accumulate. An array of R × C processing elements covers a slab of that box each cycle. Everything about utilization comes from how well slabs tile the box. The lab above shows exactly this.

The three dimensions are not equal

This is the insight that separates good reasoning from bad.

M is usually fillable. Rows do not interact. You can raise M with batching, with sequence length during prefill, or with speculative tokens during decode.

N is usually fillable. More output features or more experts or more heads give you more columns.

K is not fillable. If a dot product only has 64 terms, you cannot find more. Roune calls it the more fundamental limit. R When K is smaller than the array's reduction depth, those PEs have nothing to do.

Mismatch math

Consider a width-W array running a problem of width w, with w < W.

Situation Utilization
Naive (w/W)²
Block-diagonal, independent sub-blocks w/W

A 64-wide problem on a 128-wide array runs at 25%, or at 50% with block-diagonal packing. R The trick needs no hardware feature, since independent matmuls can occupy the upper-left and lower-right blocks of the array at the same time.

Rounding up also costs. A dimension just over a multiple is the worst case: 257 on a width of 256 uses two tiles, so it can run at half speed. R This is why you hear rules like "powers of 2 are right, otherwise your code's a blight". R

Where shapes come from

Operation M N K Notes
Feed-forward, prefill Tokens 4 × d_model d_model All large, a systolic array's friend
Feed-forward, decode Batch × speculated tokens 4 × d_model d_model M is the problem
Attention scores QKᵀ, prefill Tokens Tokens head_dim K is small
Attention scores, decode Queries per KV group Context head_dim Both M and K small
Attention output PV, decode Queries per KV group head_dim Context K large, M small
First image layer Pixels Channels 3 K=3, do it on a CPU
Depthwise 3×3 convolution Many Many 9 Poor fit for arrays, use vector units

Attention K is typically 16 to 128. Feed-forward K can be 8,192 or more. R A chip that serves both faces a 100× spread in its most important dimension.

The rows-needed equation

For a weight-stationary array with R reduction rows, loading a new weight tile takes time. While it loads, the array must stream enough activation rows to stay busy. With double buffering:

M_min = R ÷ ρ

ρ is the bandwidth available for weights, relative to activations. R With equal bandwidth, a 128×128 array needs 128 rows. One row gets 1/128 = 0.8%.

Doubling weight bandwidth halves the required rows, but you must provision that bandwidth in SRAM and HBM too. Taking this to the limit gives a batch=1 chip that needs R times as much bandwidth per operation. At that point it is no longer really a systolic array, and it needs SRAM in place of HBM. R Groq is this kind of design. It makes a deliberate trade: a much higher price for much lower token latency.

So there are three separate questions for a decode chip:

  1. How many rows can I afford to gather? This is limited by latency and KV cache.
  2. How much weight bandwidth can I pay for? This is limited by cost.
  3. What array width follows from those two?

Non-square arrays

Square arrays are the easiest for software because all vectors have one width. But each dimension can be examined separately. R

Raising K alone is roughly two arrays plus a vector add, without the vector add. It helps feed-forward and not attention, and it reduces the maximum parallelism: model K of 16,384 with array K of 1,024 allows at most 16-way within-layer splitting.

Raising N alone is roughly two arrays sharing their activation input. It saves some on-chip bandwidth. Vectors become mismatched, which complicates software.

Lowering the required M by adding weight bandwidth reduces batch and latency without changing throughput. It therefore helps responsiveness, and does nothing for tokens per dollar.

A cleverly shaped array is a way of matching your hardware to the box you expect. It also fixes your assumptions into silicon, for the two to three years it takes to design, build and deploy a chip. J

Working through a real shape

Say you serve a model with d_model = 8192 on a 256×256 weight-stationary array.

Feed-forward up-projection in decode. M = 64 users × 4 tokens = 256, N = 32768, K = 8192.

  • K tiles: 32. N tiles: 128. Each tile sees 256 rows, which matches the 256 needed.
  • Result: full utilization in steady state. This is why Roune speaks of batch 256 or batch 64 with speculation for a 256-wide array. R

Attention scores in decode, head_dim 128, 8 KV groups, 128 heads. Queries per group = 128 ÷ 8 × 4 speculated = 64. So M = 64, K = 128.

  • K of 128 on a 256-deep array: half the rows are idle unless you pack block-diagonally.
  • M of 64 against 256 needed: one quarter.
  • Result: around 12.5% to 25%, which may be fine because attention is limited by memory anyway. D

Now you can see Roune's argument for smaller attention cores: width 64 would run this same work near full utilization.

Questions to ask of any shape

  1. What are the smallest K and M I must run well?
  2. Which dimension am I relying on batching to fill, and what does that cost in latency and KV cache?
  3. What happens at non-multiples of the array width?
  4. Can independent sub-problems share the array block-diagonally?
  5. Is this operation compute-bound anyway? If it is memory-bound, low array utilization may cost nothing.

That last question matters. Utilization is not a virtue in itself. An array that sits idle while waiting on a saturated memory system is simply the correct outcome of a memory-bound workload.

Test yourself

Use the lab above to answer these. Set the array to 128×128.

  • With M=1, N=4096, K=4096, what limits you, and why does a 16×16 array do better on utilization and worse on time?
  • With K=64, how much does raising array size hurt, and what do you lose by shrinking it instead?
  • With M=257, watch what padding does, and compare with M=256.
PreviousSystolic arraysNextReduction trees

The compute core

Reduction trees

A dot product is multiplies followed by a sum. How you lay out that sum is one of the deepest structural choices in a matrix engine. Most of this chapter is O and D, because the PDFs define these blocks without analyzing them. The reasoning here connects those definitions to array design.

Two ways to add N numbers

A chain adds one number at a time. It needs N−1 adders, depth N−1, and only local wires.

A tree adds pairs, then pairs of pairs. It also needs N−1 adders, but depth is log₂N. It needs wires that get longer at each level.

Inputs Chain depth Tree depth
4 3 2
16 15 4
256 255 8
4096 4095 12

The adder count is identical. You are choosing between latency and wire complexity.

An array column is a chain in space

In a weight-stationary array, a column of R PEs is a pipelined adder chain. Each PE adds its product to the partial sum coming from above and passes it down. The depth of R adders does not hurt throughput, because each stage works on a different row. It adds R cycles of latency, and that is your fill time.

So a systolic array chooses the chain, and trades latency for short wires. With pipelining, the throughput is the same as a tree, and every wire is one PE long.

A tensor core does the opposite inside. It takes a group of products and sums them through a small tree in one step. Roune treats both as systolic arrays of different sizes, because at the chip level they play the same role. R At the circuit level they are different structures, and understanding the difference tells you what each is good at.

The grouped processing element

Here is the design knob that bridges them. Rather than one multiply per PE, put G multipliers in each PE and sum them with a small tree.

G MACs per PE Pipeline flops per MAC (int8, OS) Tree depth Clock pressure
1 1 48 0 Lowest
2 2 32 1 Low
4 4 24 2 Medium
8 8 20 3 High

The arithmetic: flops per MAC = 16 + 32/G, because each multiplier needs 16 operand-register bits and the whole group shares one 32-bit accumulator. D Fewer flops per MAC means less area, less clock power and less wire traffic. In exchange, the critical path gets longer, and a wider operand bus needs to reach each PE.

Real designs land between the extremes, because a pure chain is register-heavy and a large tree is wire-heavy.

Carry-save: why trees are cheaper than they look

Adding two numbers fully requires a carry to ripple across all the bits. Adding many numbers does not need that at each step. A carry-save adder takes three numbers and outputs two, with no carry propagation, in the delay of one full adder. E

So a multi-operand sum runs like this:

  1. Compress rows with carry-save adders, 3 to 2, again and again. Wallace and Dadda trees are two ways to arrange this. E
  2. Do one real carry-propagate addition at the end, using a fast parallel-prefix adder like Kogge-Stone or Brent-Kung. E

Inside a multiplier, the same structure reduces partial products. Booth recoding halves how many partial products you start with. E

This has a useful implication. In a grouped PE, you can feed all G products into one compressor tree and only pay for a single carry-propagate add. Better still, keep the accumulator in carry-save form across cycles, and resolve it once at readout. That shortens the critical path of a MAC considerably. The cost is roughly twice the accumulator flops.

Accumulator width

Integer accumulation has an exact bit-growth rule.

accumulator bits = a_bits + b_bits + ⌈log₂ K⌉

Operands K Bits needed D
int8 × int8 64 22
int8 × int8 256 24
int8 × int8 4096 28
int8 × int8 65536 32

Your ACC_W = 32 handles K up to 65,536 with no overflow. For your tiny GPT-2, the largest K is 256, so 24 bits would do. That cuts 8 flops from every PE, or about 17% of the PE's flops. Roune adds that sums can be made to saturate, which allows narrower accumulators with a defined failure mode. R

Accumulator width is a major hidden cost at low precision. As multipliers get smaller, the accumulator becomes a larger share of the PE. At FP4, the sum can cost more than the product. R

Floating-point accumulation

Floating-point addition needs an exponent compare, a mantissa align, an add, a normalize and a round. E A tree of full FP adders is expensive. So dot-product hardware usually does this instead:

  1. Find the largest exponent among the G products.
  2. Shift all mantissas to align with it.
  3. Add them as integers in a tree.
  4. Normalize once at the end.

This is much cheaper, but it changes rounding, and results depend on the group size. Reproducibility and numerical behavior therefore become hardware design decisions. The TPU requirement of strict deterministic repeatability shows up at this level. J

Reduction happens at every level

The same structure repeats at every scale, and the same chain-versus-tree trade applies.

Level Structure Example
Inside a multiplier Compressor tree Partial products
Inside a PE Small adder tree Grouped dot product
Across a column Pipelined chain Weight-stationary partial sums
Across K tiles Accumulator memory Summing tile results
Across lanes Log-depth shuffle tree Softmax max and sum, LayerNorm mean
Across chips Ring or tree collective All-reduce

K-splitting: using trees to fix a shape problem

When M is tiny, like decode at batch 1, a normal array leaves most rows idle. There is another option. Split K across the array, so that each row or PE group computes a partial dot product of the same output, then combine them with a reduction tree at the edge.

This turns a GEMV into full-width work. It requires bandwidth to supply K-sliced weights to every PE, since no weight gets reused across rows. That is the design point of low-batch chips: wide memory plus reduction trees, rather than an array with deep reuse.

For your embedded GPT-2, this matters, as the Your chip chapter shows.

Vector reductions

Softmax needs a max and a sum across a row. LayerNorm needs a mean and a variance. These run on lanes, so you need cross-lane reduction. Options:

  • A log-depth shuffle network across lanes. Fast, needs shuffle wiring.
  • A dedicated reduction unit at the array edge. TPUs have units for row reductions, transposes and permutes beside the array. J
  • Reusing the matrix unit by multiplying by a ones vector. Works, but wasteful.

Network reductions

All-reduce is the top-level reduction. Precision matters here too, because partial sums cross the network. Eight bits is probably too few, 32 is more than you need, and 16 is probably fine with care. Choosing 32-bit sums doubles network bandwidth, and thus network cost. R

Ironwood's SparseCores now offload collectives such as all-reduce, plus Top-K. J Your factbook notes TPU 8i adds a dedicated Collectives Acceleration Engine, which shows that reductions keep earning dedicated hardware. F

Tuning reference

Knob Effect Cost
Group size G Fewer flops per MAC Longer critical path, wider buses
Carry-save accumulators Shorter MAC path About 2× accumulator flops, resolve step
Accumulator width Fewer flops Risk of overflow, needs saturation
Saturating sums Narrower safe datapath Extra logic, changed numerics
Reduced FP alignment Cheaper FP dot product Rounding differs
Edge reduction tree Decode efficiency Area, weight bandwidth
