Feeding the array

Crossbars and networks on chip

Data rarely starts where it is needed. On-chip fabrics move it. The most useful sentence on this topic comes from Irrational Analysis: memory, whether a block of SRAM or an HBM stack, is just a node on the network on chip, so how you set up that network matters a lot. IA

Roune adds the mental tool that makes this tractable: think of the math, and remember it has to happen on a 2D plane. R

The three basic topologies

Ring Mesh Crossbar
Wires Scale with P Scale with P Scale with P²
Average hops P/4 About (2/3)·√P 1
Bisection 2 links √P links P/2 links
Latency High for large P Medium Lowest
Example AMD CCD Sapphire Rapids, inside an Nvidia GPC Ironwood core NoC, Nvidia above GPCs

Rings are simple and cheap. Each stop adds a hop, so they suit a small number of agents. AMD's Genoa-X uses nested rings: a ring within each 8-core chiplet, and those chiplets connect through a central I/O die. IA

Meshes scale well, and suit a tiled floorplan. Wires are short and regular. Sapphire Rapids uses a mesh with a memory controller and accelerators as mesh nodes, so DRAM data takes several hops to reach middle cores. IA

Crossbars connect any input to any output in one step. They are flexible and fast. They are also expensive, as the encyclopedia notes: their wiring and area costs grow quickly with port count. E

Real chips mix these. Nvidia uses meshes inside graphics processing clusters, with a crossbar tying them together. A crossbar can group a cluster that then joins a ring or mesh. Not every element needs a path to every other element. IA

Why crossbars grow as P²

A crossbar has one crosspoint for every input-output pair. With P ports of width W bits, you need P² × W crosspoints, or an equivalent tree of multiplexers. The worse problem is wiring: all P × W bits must physically cross the middle of the block.

Estimate the block's width from wiring alone:

width ≈ P × W × wire_pitch ÷ routing_layers

Example: 64 ports × 512 bits = 32,768 wires. At an 80 nm pitch on 4 layers, that is 0.66 mm of pure wire before any logic, in each direction. DO It also means long wires and more cycles of latency. Doubling ports doubles that width and quadruples the area.

Where crossbars appear in AI chips

  • SRAM banks to lanes. Letting any lane read any bank.
  • Inside every router. A NoC router is a small crossbar with buffers and an allocator. E
  • Permute units. Lane shuffles and transposes.
  • Between cores. Ironwood's memory and DMA interconnect. IA
  • In the system. NVSwitch is a crossbar for whole GPUs. R

Banks and conflicts

SRAM with many ports is expensive, so a wide memory is built from many single-port banks with a fabric in front of them. Now two requesters can collide on the same bank.

Under uniform random access, P requesters over B banks serve this many requests per cycle:

served = B × (1 − (1 − 1/B)^P)

Requesters Banks Throughput per requester D
16 16 64%
16 32 80%
16 64 89%

Random access wastes a third of your bandwidth with equal banks and requesters. Designers fix this in several ways:

  • Provision extra banks. Two banks per port reaches 80%.
  • Hash the address. XOR bits so that strides spread across banks. E
  • Pad arrays. A row stride that is not a multiple of the bank count avoids systematic conflicts.
  • Make access deterministic. Tile layouts so that software guarantees no conflicts. This is how a compiler-managed scratchpad earns its keep.

In a well-scheduled matmul, there should be no random access at all. Conflict-free layouts let you drop much of the fabric. This is one more place where software capability buys hardware simplicity.

Cheaper than a crossbar

Option Cost Limits
Full crossbar P² None
Clos, three stages About P^1.5 More latency
Beneš or butterfly P log P Permutations only, needs routing setup
Fixed shuffle P Only the patterns you chose
Time-multiplexing Lower width Lower throughput
Private banks per client None No sharing

Ask what traffic you truly need. An array that only needs transposes and row shifts can use a permutation network far cheaper than a crossbar. E

Router anatomy

A NoC router contains input buffers, route computation, a virtual-channel allocator, a switch allocator and a small crossbar. E Each element exists for a specific reason.

  • Virtual channels stop one stalled packet from blocking others on a link, and can break deadlock cycles.
  • Credits stop a sender from overrunning buffers when feedback takes several cycles. E
  • Escape channels give a proven path to forward progress. E
  • Allocators resolve contention each cycle.

Each is hardware that exists because traffic is unpredictable.

Determinism removes the machinery

Groq's slides list what it dropped: no arbiters, no reactive components, no reordering, and no link-layer replay. Functional units are stateless and side-effect free, and data moves on fixed stream registers in one of two directions. Instruction dispatch takes under 3% of the area. IA

That is the logical end of this line of thought. If a compiler knows every data movement on every cycle, you need no buffers for contention, no allocators and no flow control. The hardware becomes simple and fast. The cost is that every chip must stay in lockstep, and the compiler must schedule the entire system.

Most designs sit somewhere between. TPUs use compiler-controlled DMAs with hardware queues. GPUs use full dynamic scheduling. The right point depends on how predictable your workload is, and AI workloads are predictable: few branches, and the ones that exist are rarely data-dependent. R Dynamic routing exists for unpredictable traffic, which matmul generally is not. MoE is the exception.

The NoC as a power consumer

Moving a byte a millimeter costs energy on every hop, and data-movement energy adds up to a large fraction of chip power. Keep producers close to consumers.

  • Place SRAM banks right next to the array edges they feed.
  • Give each array its own local memory, with the global fabric carrying only what must be shared.
  • Size fabric bandwidth to steady-state flow, then add margin for bursts.

Tuning reference

Knob Effect Cost
Port count More parallel clients Quadratic in a crossbar
Port width More bandwidth Wiring, linear in width
Hierarchy levels Keeps crossbars small Non-uniform latency
Banks per port Fewer conflicts Area overhead per bank
Address hashing Removes stride conflicts Small logic, harder debug
Router buffers Absorb bursts Area, leakage
Virtual channels Avoid blocking More buffers and allocators
Static schedule Removes arbitration Compiler effort, brittle
PreviousReduction treesNextMemory

Feeding the array

Memory

If the systolic array is the engine, memory is the fuel system. This chapter covers how designers size each level, and what each level is for.

The pyramid

Going up the hierarchy gives exponentially better performance at much higher cost. IA

Level Typical size Bandwidth What it holds
PE registers Bytes per PE Highest Operands in flight
Accumulators KB to MB Very high Partial sums
Register file KB to MB Very high Vectors
Scratchpad or L1 100s of KB to 100s of MB High Tiles
HBM 10s to 100s of GB TB/s Weights, KV cache
Host or SSD TB GB/s Cold KV cache, checkpoints

Cache or scratchpad

If hardware decides what stays in on-chip memory, it is a cache. If software decides, it is a scratchpad. Public discussion gets this wrong constantly, and the difference changes memory maps, hardware complexity and the programming model. IA

Cache Scratchpad
Who places data Hardware, by guessing Software, explicitly
Extra hardware Tags, replacement, coherence DMA engines
Timing Varies with hits and misses Deterministic
Good when Access is irregular Access is known in advance

Roune adds a useful twist. Automatic caches are convenient for normal code. In high-performance code, you already think about what is in cache, so manual control is actually more convenient. R His recommendation is both: a cache that is automatic by default, with portions convertible to manual. Nvidia GPUs have both already, through L1 and shared memory.

Jouppi lists software control of the memory hierarchy through DMAs and scratchpads as one of the six key decisions. J TPU cores access memory only through DMA. R

Sizing SRAM from first principles

Step 1: the reuse you need

Take a matmul where an output tile of size Tm × Tn accumulates on chip while K streams through. Bytes moved for each step of K are (Tm + Tn) × b. Operations are 2 × Tm × Tn. So:

intensity = 2·Tm·Tn ÷ ((Tm + Tn)·b)

For a square tile of side T, intensity is T ÷ b. To reach the machine's ridge point, you need:

T ≥ ridge × b

For Ironwood in BF16, the ridge is 316 FLOP/byte, so T ≥ 632. D That tile's FP32 accumulators take only 1.6 MB. Square tiles of that size are small next to 128 MiB, so raw matmul reuse is not what forces large SRAM.

Step 2: double buffering

To overlap compute with data movement, you hold the current tile and load the next one. E

SRAM ≥ 2 × (Tm·Tk + Tk·Tn) × b + Tm·Tn × acc_bytes

Multiply by the number of arrays sharing the SRAM. The software pipeline's stages decide how many buffers you need. Each live operation costs real storage, which is why fewer pipeline stages are preferred. R

Step 3: what actually consumes capacity

Most of a real scratchpad goes to things beyond one tile:

  • Weights resident across many tokens.
  • Fused operations holding intermediate activations, which saves round trips to HBM.
  • KV tiles during attention.
  • Staging for collectives, so that network traffic never touches HBM. R

Your factbook shows Google's split: TPU 8t has 128 MB of vector SRAM, while the serving-focused 8i has 384 MB. F Serving spends silicon on SRAM because decode has less reuse to exploit.

Bank organization

A 128 MiB scratchpad is many thousands of small macros. Macro size trades density against speed. Larger macros have less peripheral overhead per bit, but longer bitlines and more energy per access. E Each access only needs a small piece, so many small banks are typical, and they also supply parallelism.

Bandwidth needed at the array edge for an R×C weight-stationary array per cycle: R activation elements in, C results out, plus weights while loading. Provision ports for that, and put the banks physically at the edge.

Why HBM

Standard DRAM was the bottleneck on TPU v1, so TPU v2 moved to HBM. J Jouppi ranks HBM third among the six key decisions, and most accelerators have converged on it.

HBM stacks DRAM dies on a base die and connects it through a silicon interposer with a very wide, relatively slow interface. Width gives you bandwidth at reasonable energy per bit. The costs are interposer area, packaging difficulty and price.

An important distinction from Roune: HBM is expensive per GB of storage, but not per GB/s of bandwidth. He estimates around 3× regular RAM per GB. R So ask whether you need the capacity or the bandwidth. They come bundled, and those are different questions.

How much capacity

Two things fill HBM: weights and KV cache.

KV bytes = 2 · batch · layers · seq · groups · width · bytes · idle · pipeline

Roune's example: batch 64, 32 layers, 1M context, 8 groups, width 128, 1 byte per element gives 4,194 GB. Split 32 ways, that is 131 GB per chip. RD This is why chips carry about 200 GB.

Weights are less of a problem than people assume. With 1,024 chips, 1,000 GB of weights is 1 GB per chip. R

The two respond differently to parallelism.

Parallelism Weights per chip KV cache per chip
Duplication Same Same
Pipelining across layers ÷S Same, for decode
Within layers ÷P ÷P

How much bandwidth

Decode reads all active weights and each user's KV cache every step. So:

step time ≥ (weight bytes + batch × KV bytes per user) ÷ bandwidth

Note that batching amortizes weights but not KV. Roune also points out that splitting across C chips does not change per-chip bandwidth need, because each chip reads 1/C of the data, and you want C times the tokens. R

Reducing the need

Roune argues this is where the biggest savings hide. R

  • Sparse or indexed attention replaces dense reads of ancient history with retrieval. Going from 1M to 1k tokens of dense attention takes KV from 4,194 GB to 4 GB. It could even allow KV on SSD.
  • Grouped-query attention cuts KV by the group factor.
  • KV quantization to 8 or 4 bits. 8 is standard for serious work.
  • Lossless compression on top of lossy quantization. JPEG does both. One reported result is about 20% size reduction. This needs Huffman decoding at memory speed in the DMA path, and Nvidia's existing decompressor runs at only about one tenth of memory speed. Lossy mapping can be folded into the same lookup tables, so a per-layer custom format can be nearly free. Roune is careful to say he has not quantified the area cost.

Stacking more SRAM

Hybrid bonding can add SRAM directly above logic. AMD's V-Cache adds 64 MB per chiplet with only a small latency cost, placed above existing SRAM, while blank silicon covers the hot cores. IA For a statically scheduled design, added latency hardly matters because the compiler accounts for it in advance, so Irrational Analysis sees this as a natural next step for Groq-style chips. IA

Latency, bandwidth and Little's law

To keep a memory pipe full, you must have enough requests in flight.

bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency

With 7.3 TB/s and a 500 ns round trip, you need 3.65 MB outstanding. At 4 KB per request, that is about 890 requests in flight. D Every queue on that path has to hold them: DMA descriptors, memory controller queues, response buffers. This is the calculation behind Roune's warning that one undersized queue can destroy performance. R

SRAM-only machines

Groq stores all weights in on-chip SRAM: 220 MB in an early part at a slide-quoted 55 TB/s, and about 500 MB in LPU3. IAR Your factbook's 128 GB across 256 LPUs per rack agrees with that figure. FD A 100B FP8 model needs at least 200 chips just for weights. R

Irrational Analysis insists this is not fundamentally about SRAM. The SRAM enables a deterministic dataflow. IA Roune's view is more economic: low batch needs enormous bandwidth, which forces SRAM, which is expensive, and that makes sense only for premium low-latency tokens. R Both are true at different levels.

Tuning reference

Knob Effect Cost
SRAM capacity Bigger tiles, more fusion, less HBM traffic Area that barely shrinks
SRAM bandwidth and banks Feed arrays, fewer conflicts Macro overhead, wiring
Buffering depth Hides latency SRAM capacity
HBM stacks Bandwidth and capacity Beachfront, cost, power
Compression in DMA Effective bandwidth and capacity Engine area, variable sizes
Queue depth Sustains bandwidth Control area
Cache mode Easier programming Tags, less determinism
PreviousCrossbars, NoCNextControl and feeding

Feeding the array

Control and feeding

Someone has to tell the array what to do on every cycle. How you answer that question decides how much of your chip is control logic, how hard your compiler is, and how predictable your machine is.

The spectrum of control

The core tradeoff: hardware that figures things out at runtime costs area and power. Software that figures things out in advance costs engineers and flexibility.

Style Who schedules Hardware cost Compiler burden Example
Out-of-order superscalar Hardware, per instruction Very high Low CPUs
SIMT with warps Hardware, per warp High Medium GPUs
Modest VLIW with DMA Compiler, per bundle Low High TPUs
Very wide static VLIW Compiler, cycle-exact, whole system Very low Extreme Groq
Fixed function Nobody, burned into silicon Lowest None Taalas, in the extreme

Fancy cores give great performance boosts, at a cost in area, power and parallelism. That is the main reason CPUs are poor at AI. IA

Why VLIW fits AI

A VLIW bundle packs several operations for different units into one instruction. The compiler must guarantee they can run together. Hardware becomes simple, and the compiler burden is heavy. IA

This suits AI because AI code has few branches, and the branches it has rarely depend on data. Everything is very regular. R Program size is small, so wider instructions are cheap, and CPU-style backward binary compatibility is unnecessary. J

TPU v2's bundle is 322 bits: 2 scalar slots, 4 vector slots (2 for load/store), 2 matrix slots (push and pop), 1 miscellaneous slot and 6 immediates. IAJ As hardware grew, Google simply widened the bundle. Ironwood's is over 50% wider. J

The sequence runs like this: scalar unit fetches the bundle, runs scalar slots, forwards decoded instructions to the vector and matrix units, which run decoupled from scalar execution. J

SIMT and what it buys

GPUs run warps of 32 threads (AMD uses waves of 64 in the datacenter) sharing one instruction. IA When a warp stalls on memory, the hardware switches to another warp. This is warp scheduling, and Roune calls it the largest part of what makes a GPU a GPU. R

His argument is that warp scheduling is hardware-implemented pipelining. The same result can come from software pipelining at less hardware cost, since AI memory access is predictable. It is an artifact of graphics heritage, where shaders do have unpredictable access. R

The other side of this argument matters too. Warp scheduling makes high performance reachable for programmers who have never heard of software pipelining. If you pipeline by hand, CUDA is far more productive. R That is a large part of why CUDA won.

Watch how GPUs have moved toward TPU-like structures: Blackwell's SM has a Tensor Memory Accelerator for bulk asynchronous copies, and dedicated Tensor Memory beside each tensor core. IA Warp specialization, where some warps only move data, is awkwardly recreating CPU-style threads inside a GPU. R

Cycle tyranny

An array consumes operands continuously. Suppose it takes one LHS vector and one RHS vector, and emits one result per cycle. Reading, writing and post-processing could mean about 10 vector operations per cycle, each 256 wide, with no gaps allowed. Roune calls this the tyranny of the cycles. R

One non-TPU chip project failed exactly here. The control core could not keep up, so the array could never reach full rate, regardless of how it was programmed. R

Ways to reduce this pressure:

Technique How it helps Cost
2D vector registers One 8×128 register carries 8 rows, so 8× fewer instructions Tiling complications
Queues around the array Burst rows in, then do other work Queue area
Slower array clock More control cycles per array cycle More arrays needed
Loop unrolling Addresses become constant offsets Code size
DMA straight into the array Control acts every few thousand cycles Custom transforms still need the vector path

An instructive story: TPU v2 engineers saw inner loops with heavy address arithmetic, and added a dedicated address unit. Nobody used it, since unrolling made those addresses constants. The sample loops were not unrolled when they measured. R This is a clear case of what the Judgement chapter calls derived consequences.

Systolic array DMAs are Roune's idea: a DMA delivers thousands of rows directly into the array from SRAM, HBM, the network or another array. It is close to a dataflow design. It breaks down when you need to transform data in transit, or when op fusion puts vector work between load and multiply. R

Software pipelining

This is the most important software concept in AI hardware. A loop has three stages, A, B and C, on different units. Run in order, only one unit is active at a time, so utilization is 33%. Overlap iterations, and all three run at once. R

Step Unit A Unit B Unit C
1 x₁
2 x₂ a₁
3 x₃ a₂ b₁
4 x₄ a₃ b₂
5 a₄ b₃
6 b₄

Twelve sequential steps become six. For S stages and N iterations, total steps are N + S − 1, and utilization in the prologue and epilogue is lower. Key rules:

  • The slowest stage sets the pace, so balance stages.
  • Prefer fewer stages. Each adds a prologue and epilogue, and needs buffers.
  • Each live operation needs resources, such as a second buffer.

The universal AI loop has three stages: load tile, compute tile, store tile. Every kernel does this. Roune's recommendation is a tiled pipelining library with declared stages and tile coordinates, so nobody writes this by hand. R

Hardware needs very little for this: a queue for memory requests. All CPUs have one. TPUs have one for DMAs. R

Synchronization

With everything asynchronous, you need to know when data has arrived.

  • Sync flags. TPU DMAs set a flag on completion, and the program stalls until it is set. J
  • Semaphores and barriers. General coordination between engines. E
  • Time. Groq's chips know the cycle on which everything happens. SYNC parks instruction queues, and NOTIFY wakes them, so all 144 queues proceed in lockstep. IA

Static scheduling at the extreme

Groq's instruction set includes operations that exist only for time: NOP n waits, DESKEW pauses until a hardware counter overflows, and a Runtime Deskew delays a chip by a small amount. IA The whole machine is plesiochronous: separate clocks at nearly the same rate, aligned through hardware and software counters. Links are paced by software, and forward error correction replaces retransmission, because a retry would break the schedule. IA

What you get: fully deterministic timing, simple hardware and high utilization. What it costs:

  • The compiler must schedule every operation in the system to the cycle.
  • If skew varies, execution stalls by design.
  • Drift, jitter and memory refresh become software problems. Groq's patents cover scheduling around DRAM refresh, yet no Groq chip has used DRAM. IA

Irrational Analysis's reversal is worth understanding. After years of calling the design an abomination, the author concluded that if the compiler works, real clock forwarding could remove the worst weakness. Nvidia's ISSCC 2026 optical link holds forwarded-clock phase variation to about 16 ps. That is an inference from an investor with disclosed positions, in an unfinished draft. It remains an interesting way to think: when one key limit gets removed, a discarded architecture can return.

Roune cautions against overrating static scheduling, since TPUs also allow careful timing, and the gain over other chips is exaggerated by marketing. R

Do you need a host?

GPUs and TPUs rely on a host CPU. Roune argues this adds cost, an extra failure domain and extra data hops, and that a chip with its own CPU cores could run Linux itself. R To stop OS interrupts from disturbing arrays, keep OS work on cores with no attached array.

Ironwood has 2,304 hosts for 9,216 chips, and hosts are its main availability challenge. J

Hardware limits are software interfaces

Every hardware limit is a question: how many DMAs in flight? How deep is this queue? How many descriptors? Early TPU teams guessed at many of these, and software teams did not know a decision had been made. R Roune's rule: hardware should never design a software-facing interface without software. And almost everything is software-facing.

Tuning reference

Knob Effect Cost
VLIW width More parallel units controlled Instruction memory
Register tile depth Less control per array vector Tiling constraints
Queue depth Decoupling, fewer stalls Area, latency
Outstanding DMAs Sustained bandwidth Tracking tables
Simple CPU cores Runs collectives, OS work Area

Feeding the array

Vector units and everything else

Most operations in a transformer run inside matmul. But the ones that do not can still decide your speed. Vector units are the sixth of Jouppi's six key decisions. J

What runs here

Operation Why the array cannot do it Hardware it wants
Softmax Exponentials, row max, row sum Exp approximation, reductions
LayerNorm, RMSNorm Mean, variance, reciprocal square root Reduction, 1/√x
GELU, SiLU Non-linear functions Polynomial or lookup
RoPE Pairwise rotation Elementwise multiply-add
Residual add Elementwise Adder, ideally fused
Quantize, dequantize Scale, round, clip Scale multiplier, saturation
Top-k, sampling Sorting, randomness Selection network
Optimizer step (training) Per-weight math Heavy vector throughput

Your PLAN.md lists exactly these: requant, LayerNorm, softmax, GELU, residual add. The encyclopedia has a block for each. E

Sizing the vector unit

Use Amdahl's law with overlap. Suppose a tile takes T_array cycles on the array, and its follow-on vector work takes T_vector cycles.

  • If they run in series, total = T_array + T_vector.
  • If software pipelined, total = max(T_array, T_vector).

You want T_vector ≤ T_array, so vector work hides completely. Vector throughput needed then follows from how many vector operations each array output needs.

Worked example. A 256×256 array in steady state produces 256 outputs per cycle. If each output needs 4 vector operations for scale, bias, activation and quantization, you need 1,024 lane-operations per cycle. D Ironwood's move to four general ALUs per lane, and vector registers going from 8×128 to 16×256, is this calculation made real. J

Attention is harder: for each score element you need a subtract, an exp, a sum and a multiply, and K is small so the array finishes quickly. This is where vector units become the critical path. FlashAttention-style tiling keeps that work on chip, and the exp unit often sets the limit. F

TPU's vector unit

TPU v2 has 128 lanes, each with an 8-way sublane dimension, so one operation covers 8 × 128 elements. Each lane reads and writes its own local slice of VMEM. J That locality matters: no crossbar is needed for the common case.

Two things evolved. ALUs grew from two restricted units per lane, each able to do some operations, to four general-purpose ones. Registers doubled in both dimensions. J

Note the design pattern. Restricted ALUs are cheap but constrain the compiler. As logic got cheaper, generality won.

Nonlinear function strategy

You rarely build exact hardware. Three options E:

  • Lookup table: fast and simple. Size grows with accuracy.
  • Polynomial with multiply-add: reuses vector ALUs. Needs several cycles.
  • Interpolated table: a small table plus one multiply-add. A good compromise.

For softmax, subtract the row max before exponentiating, for numerical range. Exponentials in base 2 reduce to a shift plus a small polynomial on the fractional part. A reciprocal unit lets you multiply rather than divide.

For fixed-point designs like yours, define the approximation identically in Python and RTL, since numerical matching is a stated risk in your plan. Nonlinear units and MoE works all of this through for your chip, with measured table sizes and errors.

Transpose and permute

Training needs high-throughput transposes in the backward pass. You could do them on the array, but a transpose unit costs far less power and area. R Inference can usually avoid them. Compute Q·Kᵀ directly with an array mode that takes the second operand transposed, as TPUs do, and transpose weights offline. R Roune recommends keeping a permute unit anyway, for head layout. He says he is less sure on transpose, and notes that you will sleep better with it.

SparseCore

SparseCore is a small dataflow engine for embeddings, taking about 5% of die area and 5% of power. Each unit has 16 tiles, each with an HBM channel, a Fetch Unit, an 8-wide SIMD unit, a Flush Unit, and a slice of 2.5 MiB Sparse Vector Memory. J

Its name misleads: it has nothing to do with structured sparsity. It is "sparse" in the sense of accessing HBM at finer granularity. R Watch how its role changed over time. Built for recommendation embeddings, it became an offload for all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast, Top-K and small sparse decode work. J Roune suggests a plain CPU core could do the same job more generally. R

The general lesson: a small second engine for irregular work is cheap insurance against a shifting workload.

Silent data corruption

Vector units are now also a reliability feature. Ironwood's hardware replay unit randomly samples vector bundles and reruns odd-lane operations on even lanes in idle VLIW slots. It adds no performance overhead, it is invisible to the compiler, and it has caught defective chips that passed every other screen. J

Systems

Workloads

An AI chip is not one kind of chip. Training, prefill and decode want different hardware, and a large part of this field comes down to one number: arithmetic intensity.

The roofline

For a given operation, arithmetic intensity is operations performed per byte moved from memory. A machine has a ridge point equal to peak FLOP/s ÷ memory bytes/s.

  • If intensity is below the ridge, you are memory-bound. Speed = intensity × bandwidth.
  • If intensity is above the ridge, you are compute-bound. Speed = peak.

Adding compute to a memory-bound workload does nothing. Adding bandwidth to a compute-bound workload does nothing. The first job in any analysis is working out which side you are on. For Ironwood, the ridge is 316 FLOP/byte in BF16. D

The three workloads

Training Prefill Decode
What it does Updates weights Reads the prompt Writes output
Tokens per step per sequence Thousands Thousands 1 to 4
Limited by Compute, if done right Compute Memory, unless heavily optimized
Extra needs Transpose, optimizer vector work, 16-bit math, flexibility Fast arrays Bandwidth, capacity for KV

Inference prices show this directly. Output tokens cost more than input tokens, even though the math per token is almost the same. R

Roune's advice to a startup is not to start with a training chip. Training needs transposition hardware, more vector compute, 16-bit numerics, more ops and more flexibility, for researchers who try new things daily. R Google also started with inference: TPU v1.

Decode: where it gets hard

Generating one token per conversation means the matmul has one row. That gives under 1% utilization on a large array, and it reads every weight and all the keys to do very little math.

Feed-forward in decode

Batching helps because users share weights. Intensity for batch B and b bytes per weight:

intensity = 2B ÷ b

So the batch needed to reach the ridge is ridge × b ÷ 2.

Chip Ridge in F/B Batch at ridge D
TPU v2, BF16 66 66
TPU v4, BF16 229 229
Ironwood, BF16 316 316
Ironwood, FP8 632 316
GB300, NVFP4 1875 469

Each generation asks for more batch. Lower precision does not change this, since it raises peak and cuts bytes per weight by the same factor. D

Attention in decode

Batching does not help attention, since each user has different keys. R What helps is sharing keys across queries:

  • Grouped-query attention. 128 heads in 8 groups gives 16 queries per key set.
  • Speculative decoding. 4 tokens at a time gives 4× more.
  • Parallel agents. Several chains of thought over the same context. R

Combined: 4 × 128 ÷ 8 = 64× reuse. R Attention intensity is 2q ÷ b for q queries per key set. With q = 64 and 1 byte per element, that is 128 FLOP/byte: much better, and still under Ironwood's ridge. D

Technique Helps FF? Helps attention? Cost
Batch Yes No Latency, KV capacity
GQA No Yes Some model quality
Speculative decode Yes Yes Wasted work on bad guesses
KV quantization No Yes Accuracy risk
Sparse attention No Yes, greatly Model work
Weight quantization Yes No Accuracy risk

Why you cannot speculate forever

Guesses come from a cheap model, and the chance of 16 correct tokens in a row falls quickly. R Why not one KV group for everybody? Model quality suffers. R Every multiplier has its limit.

Prefill

All tokens are known, so you process them at once. Each key gets reused thousands of times, and memory bandwidth is rarely the issue. The problem becomes the K dimension in attention: GQA models usually widen key vectors, which helps fill the array. R

RAG means models read more than they write, so Roune expects most future tokens to be prefill. That would keep arrays important even as decode gets the attention. R

Mixing prefill and decode

Strategy Idea Tradeoff
Default aggregation Same chip, unmanaged mix Unpredictable balance
Disaggregation Separate chips, moving KV between them Specialized hardware, transfer cost
Managed aggregation (chunked prefill) Mix in a fixed ratio on one chip Needs a scheduler, but uses both resources fully

The third is elegant. A memory-bound decode batch and a compute-bound prefill chunk use different resources, so running them together fills both. You could even provision less bandwidth, which is a risky bet on customer software. R Overlapping attention with feed-forward works the same way.

Google's 8t and 8i split is disaggregation at the product level. Nvidia pairing LPUs for decode FF with GPUs for attention and prefill is disaggregation within one model. FR

What software changes

Almost every provisioning answer depends on software, and answers can differ by 10× or 100×. R A chip for perfect software and a chip for arbitrary software are different products. This is the single largest source of disagreement between experts on this topic. Each side has a point: the empirical studies measure what is deployed today, and the hardware architects reason about what could be deployed.

Other model families

Your factbook covers cases that do not fit this picture: state-space models with fixed-size recurrent state, diffusion language models, and hybrid attention. F Depthwise convolutions in Mamba models have K as small as 9 and run badly on big arrays, so they belong on vector units. R Architectures that replace attention would change KV math entirely.

Skeptics warned that ASICs would go out of date with AI's pace. Transformers went from a paper in December 2017 to 21% of Google's workload just 15 months later, and 74% by 2026. J TPU v2's architecture handled that shift because it was built on general matmul, vector units and programmable control. Designing for a stable abstraction is the defense against this risk.

PreviousVector unitsNextScale-out

Systems

Scale-out

A chip is only part of the machine. Roune calls parallelization tricky and unintuitive, and he admits he and others got it wrong for a long time, leading to an overprovisioned TPU network. R Take this chapter slowly.

The concepts

  • Throughput: tokens per second across all users.
  • Token latency: ms per token for one user. Different from first-token latency.
  • Local vs global: per-chip against total. A 1 TB model does fit on 20 chips with 100 GB each.
  • Minimum installation: chips required before anything runs.
  • Failure domain: what stops working if one part fails.

Latency and throughput are not related in any simple way. Almost all published material quotes one without the other, which makes the number close to meaningless. R

The parallelism table

This is the core of the chapter. S = pipeline stages, P = within-layer ways, D = copies. R

Type Throughput Token latency Weights per chip KV per chip Network need Failure domain
Duplication ×D ×D Same Same Same Little Better
Pipeline ×S, decode, partial Under ×S Up ÷S Same Critical ×S
Pipeline ×S, decode, full ×S ×2 ÷S ×2 Only needs to finish in a layer time ×S
Pipeline ×S, prefill ×S ×2 if full ÷S ÷S Low ×S
Within layer ×P ×P ÷P, roughly ÷P ÷P High ×P

Three surprising facts

1. Network bandwidth limits within-layer parallelism. Between-layer traffic is far lighter.

2. Double the network and you can as much as halve token latency, through twice the within-layer split. So large arrays, which raise batch and latency, are a force for faster networks.

3. Pipelining helps weights but not decode KV cache. Each chip stores only its layers' keys, which divides by S. But you now need S times as many conversations in flight to keep all stages busy. The two factors cancel. Prefill avoids this, since stages can work on spans of one document. R

Within-layer math

Attention splits by heads: GQA groups stay together, giving maybe 8 ways, and splitting the KV across chips adds maybe 8 more, for about 64 total. Feed-forward splits on the wide hidden dimension: 16k × 4 ÷ 256 = 256 chips at full array utilization. R

Each layer ends with an all-reduce. For data size X on P chips:

bytes per chip = 2X(1 − 1/P)

That barely depends on P. So why does doubling P more than double bandwidth need? Because each chip now finishes in half the time, so all-reduces arrive twice as often. Per-chip network rate scales with P. R

Hiding it. Run two half-batches: one computes while the other communicates. That doubles latency and KV, and removes network waits. Suppose you are 8-way with 25% network overhead. Pipelining lets you go to 32-way with no waits. Latency doubles, then falls 4×: net half the latency. R

Precision on the wire. 32-bit sums need twice the bandwidth of 16-bit sums. R

Mixture of experts

Each token goes to a few of many experts. Mixtral uses 2 of 8. Llama 4 Maverick has 128 experts with 17B of 400B weights active, about 4%. R Problems:

  • Uneven load. A 120% load on an expert needs two copies, each 60% busy. 1020% needs 11 copies at 93%. Large deployments smooth this out. R
  • Not enough rows. Each expert sees only its share of the batch, so it struggles to fill an array.
  • All-to-all traffic. Tokens travel to arbitrary chips.

On a single chip at batch 1 these problems mostly vanish, and only the storage cost stays. Nonlinear units and MoE works that case through.

Priority queues help: high-priority tokens go first, and batch work fills spare capacity. R Forced even routing gives full utilization at a cost in answer quality, since a token may get the wrong expert. R

Link types

Shorter links give more bandwidth per dollar. In order: R

  1. Same die
  2. Silicon bridge or interposer
  3. Package pin
  4. Passive copper trace
  5. Active copper trace
  6. Board-to-board connector
  7. Backplane
  8. Flexible copper cable
  9. Optical cable

Water cooling lets boards sit closer, so links get shorter and cheaper. Air cooling and routers push links longer. R

Be suspicious of any single bandwidth number. Is it bits or bytes? One direction or both? Giga or gibi? Line rate or payload? Theoretical or measured? R Jouppi quotes per-direction numbers, and explains others would double them. J

The efficiency formula

useful bandwidth per chip = link utilization × total link bandwidth ÷ average hops

A router is a node, and it is not a useful destination. Every bit traverses chip → router → chip, so average hops is 2. A single router wastes half its bandwidth. R Multiple levels waste more. In a torus where only neighbors communicate, hops can be 1.

All-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce can all run with only neighbor traffic. So for dense models a torus runs twice as fast as a router for the same link hardware, with no router to buy. R A mesh without wraparound links runs at half the speed of a torus. R

Topologies

Topology Hops, neighbors Hops, random Cost Used by
Single router 2 1.5 at 4 nodes, 2 at many Router plus longer links NVLink domain
1D torus, 4 wide 1 1 None Early NVLink, Roune's ring boards
4×4 torus 1 2 None Roune's donut
4×4×4 torus 1 3 None Google's cube
16×16×24 torus 1 14 None TPU v5p large slice
Dragonfly Groups fully connected Small High-radix Groq, future TPUs

Random traffic gets worse with torus size, since average distance per dimension is width ÷ 4. So MoE is fine on small tori and poor on huge ones. R Tokens going to many experts, or within-expert parallelism, shift things back toward tori.

Nvidia's NVL72 gives every GPU a single hop to every other at full bandwidth, over passive copper. It is the best in performance and flexibility, and worst in cost and reliability. IA Google's torus is more reliable and cost-effective, but it asks compilers to handle non-uniform topology. IA

Google's optical circuit switches

Rack: 4×4×4 = 64 chips in electrically wired cubes, a size chosen because 3D cubes have the best bisection and 64 chips plus 16 hosts fit in a rack. J Inside a cube, links use PCB traces and copper cables, 144 in all, and only cube faces go optical. IAD Each cube face has 16 links, so 96 optical links per cube. Opposing faces go to the same switch, so 48 switches connect all cubes. Each switch has 136 ports: 128 plus 8 spares. J

MEMS mirrors switch in milliseconds, which sounds slow. They are not routing packets. They rewire topology around failures and between jobs. Benefits: J

  • Fault isolation. Route around a bad cube.
  • Scheduling. A 128-chip job takes any two cubes, not 128 contiguous chips.
  • Incremental deployment. A cube works once its 64 chips are installed.
  • Odd sizes. That is why Ironwood has 9,216 chips: four 2K jobs plus 16 spare cubes.

Roune considers this more expensive than necessary, and proposes a cheaper design: 4×4 tori on copper, connected through cheap low-bandwidth routers, in an N×4×4 topology. R Whether that wins depends on cost data neither of us has.

Pod shape, recovered from a table

A torus bisection is 2 × (smallest cross-section) × link bandwidth. Using that on Table 1 recovers shapes the paper never states. D

Generation Chips Shape that fits Bisection check
TPU v2 256 16×16 2 × 16 × 62 = 1,984 GB/s
TPU v3 1,024 32×32 2 × 32 × 70 = 4,480
TPU v4 4,096 16×16×16 2 × 256 × 50 = 25,600
TPU v5p 8,960 16×20×28 2 × 320 × 100 = 64,000
Ironwood 9,216 16×24×24 2 × 384 × 100 = 76,800

All five match the published bisection exactly. That is a strong check, though these shapes are inferred and not confirmed by the paper.

Reliability

Parallelism multiplies failure rates: if one of 1,024 chips stopping halts the job, the system is 1,024 times as fragile. In early TPU pods, one failed cable took down a whole pod until someone walked over to replace it. Sameer Kumar's fix made software work around missing links, at half the torus bandwidth, which happened to be available because the network was overprovisioned. R Accidental margin turned out to be useful.

Silent data corruption is harder, because nothing fails visibly. Ironwood's defenses: FBIST inside the MXU for functional self-test, and hardware replay on the VPU. J

The goodput target is 93% across multiple pods. Five features support this: better nodes, error checking, checkpoint and restore, strict deterministic repeatability, and modular isolation. J

Simulate this

Roune has a PhD in computer algebra, and he got this math wrong for an embarrassingly long time. He recommends simulating parallelism, not only using a spreadsheet. R Even simulation is not enough: TPU v3's first silicon could not drive its cables at all, despite simulation, and a week of work by the firmware and hardware teams saved the launch. R

Generations

This is how real designers improved their architectures. The best way to learn reasoning is to watch the same machine move through eight years of changing constraints. Google published the numbers, so we can check what happened.

What changed at each step, and why

TPU v1: the inference chip

A nearly pure int8 array driven by a host, with DRAM as its bottleneck. JR Motivation was modest: speech synthesis would have been too expensive to run on existing hardware. R It gave 30× the performance per watt of contemporary GPUs and showed the idea worked. J

v1 to v2: becoming a computer

Training changes everything. v2 added BF16 multiplies with FP32 accumulation, HBM for about 30× more memory bandwidth, vector units, a VLIW scalar core and ICI links. J v1's single 256-wide int8 array became two 128-wide BF16 arrays. The team was about 30 people. R Many things were overprovisioned, including the network. R

This block diagram still describes Ironwood. Getting that structure right was the most valuable decision in the line.

v2 to v3: the cheap upgrade

Doubling MXUs, a clock increase of 34%, liquid cooling. HBM stacks doubled, while bandwidth rose only 29%. Pod grew 4×. Peak rose 2.7× while HBM bandwidth rose 1.3×, so the ridge doubled, using up some v2 margin.

The clock increase came with trouble: thermal surprise, a compiler fix worth 25% of clock, and a networking bug in first silicon. R

v3 to v4: the scale-out generation

Doubling MXUs again, but the big changes were at system level. 3D torus, optical circuit switches, SparseCore count doubled. Link count rose from 4 to 6, with per-link speed dropping from 70 to 50 GB/s. J That is the kind of move that only makes sense if topology matters more than raw link speed. Megacore let the compiler treat two cores as one. J

v4 to v5p: the correction

MXU count stayed the same, and clock jumped 67%. VMEM quadrupled, HBM capacity tripled, bandwidth rose 2.3×, link speed doubled. J

This is the rebalancing generation. Ridge fell from 229 to 166, the only time it fell. VMEM per TFLOP more than doubled. The v4 machine had drifted out of balance and v5p corrected it, perhaps because large models had grown and needed the capacity. This is my reading of the numbers; the paper does not say so.

v5p to Ironwood: the big jump

Array side doubled to 256, with native FP8. BF16 peak rose 5×. Other changes: J

  • Two compute dies per package. Eight HBM3E stacks.
  • Vector registers from 8×128 to 16×256.
  • Four general ALUs per lane, up from two restricted ones.
  • Redundant MXU row for yield.
  • FBIST and hardware replay.
  • SparseCore 2.4× faster, and more general.

Ridge jumped back up to 316. ICI per TFLOP fell 5×, because link speed stayed at 100 GB/s. Per-chip TDP nearly doubled.

Peak performance per TDP watt rose about 6× in this one step, far more than in any previous generation. J That mostly reflects bigger arrays, FP8 and a newer node. It uses peak numbers, as the paper notes, and the headline 100× per-node figure compares BF16 to FP8. At equal BF16 precision, it is 50×. J

After Ironwood: the split

Your factbook records that TPU 8t and 8i split training and serving into separate designs. F

8t (training) 8i (serving)
Topology 3D torus Boardfly
Vector SRAM 128 MB 384 MB
HBM 216 GB 288 GB
HBM bandwidth 6.5 TB/s 8.6 TB/s
Special block SparseCore Collectives Acceleration Engine

Everything earlier in this guide predicted this split: serving wants more memory and more SRAM, and MoE traffic favors something other than a huge torus.

What stayed the same

Equally important. Across five generations, these did not change: J

  • Two TensorCores per chip.
  • Four chips per board.
  • Systolic arrays, scratchpad, DMA, VLIW.
  • XLA as the compiler.

The paper's central claim is that this stability is a feature. Compilers and models carry forward, and tuned models are ready on day one. J

Nvidia's parallel path

Generation Year Change Source
Volta 2017 First tensor cores, 4×4 R
Turing 2018 16×16, int8 R
Ampere 2020 2:4 structured sparsity R
Hopper 2022 FP8 RO
Blackwell 2025 64×64, FP4, NVFP4, two dies R
Blackwell Ultra 2025 288 GB HBM3E, 8 TB/s, 15 PF dense NVFP4 IA

The array sizes are Roune's description. Nvidia does not publish tensor cores in these terms, so treat them as his model of the structure.

Nvidia's scale-up link has its own steady curve, from a slide in IA:

NVLink Year GB/s per GPU Domain
1 2016 160 Hybrid cube mesh
2 2018 300 First NVSwitch, 8 GPUs
3 2020 600 Ampere
4 2022 900 Hopper
5 2024 1,800 Blackwell, 72 GPUs all-to-all
6 2026 3,600 Rubin

Compare this with TPU's ICI, whose per-chip total went from 248 to 600 GB/s over the same period. Nvidia spends far more on per-chip link bandwidth. Google spends on topology instead, and keeps links neighbor-only. Those are two different answers to the same parallelism problem. D

Where TPUs scaled a fixed design, Nvidia kept a general programmable core and added AI features to it. Over time it took on TPU-like traits:

  • Larger matrix units, from 4×4 toward 64×64.
  • Tensor Memory Accelerator for bulk asynchronous copies, which is effectively DMA.
  • Tensor Memory, giving accumulators dedicated storage outside the register file. An SM has 4 partitions, each with a 16,384 × 32-bit register file and 64 KB of tensor memory, and 256 KB of shared L1. IA
  • Warp specialization, which is close to separating data-movement and compute threads. R

Meanwhile TPUs became more programmable, with general ALUs, Pallas kernels and C++-like control. The two architectures are moving toward the same place from opposite sides. Roune sees the endpoint as a CPU with a large array. R

Nvidia led on numerics and sparsity from FP8 on, while Google led earlier with large arrays and BF16. R

Groq's different bet

Groq chose determinism as its organizing idea. Hot Chips 2022 describes a chip viewable as a 144-wide VLIW, with 320-element vectors built from 20 superlanes of 16 lanes each, and about 220 MB of flat SRAM. IA LPU3 reaches about 500 MB. R Nvidia licensed the technology and hired the team for about $20B, per Irrational Analysis. It is positioned for premium, low-latency decode FF, with GPUs doing attention and prefill. RIA Your factbook has Groq 3 LPX in production as of August 2026, with 256 LPUs per rack. F

Principles you can extract

1. Fix the interface. Change the implementation. Software sees stable abstractions, while the implementation scales underneath.

2. Scale the cheapest lever first. Arrays grew. SRAM could not. Bandwidth grew when it had to.

3. Balance drifts, then gets corrected. Each generation spends the margin the last one left. Watch your ratios.

4. Spend transistors on software's problems. Google widened VLIW slots, generalized ALUs and improved DMAs as logic got cheap. Generality pays once logic stops being scarce. J

5. Move reliability into silicon as scale grows. Spare rows, self-test and replay were not needed at 256 chips. They are at 9,216.

6. Let new constraints change the metric. Performance per dollar became performance per watt, and then carbon per FLOP. J

7. Margin has value. Overprovisioned networks saved TPU pods when cables failed. R A perfectly balanced chip has nowhere to absorb a surprise.

The six decisions

Jouppi ranks what proved most durable. J

  1. Systolic arrays for matrix multiplies.
  2. Range-oriented narrow floating point.
  3. HBM for main memory.
  4. Custom high-speed links.
  5. Software control of the memory hierarchy, with DMAs and scratchpads.
  6. Vector units for non-matrix computation.

Two other innovations remain unique to TPUs: optical switches and SparseCores. There is still no agreement across the industry on processors per accelerator, from 2 up to 1,472. J Cray's old question captures Google's position: would you rather plow a field with two strong oxen or 1,024 chickens? J

Practice

Method: from goal to architecture

Here is the procedure, with three worked examples. Every number comes from model/ or is a stated assumption.

The procedure

Step 1. Write the workload down

List model sizes, layer shapes, precision, context, target token rate and cost metric. Decide whether you control the software.

Step 2. List every matmul shape

Write M, N, K for each operation. Note the smallest K and smallest M you must run well. These set your array width.

Step 3. Find intensity at your batch

Compute FLOPs and bytes per step. Compare to candidate ridge points. This tells you whether you are buying compute, bandwidth or capacity.

Step 4. Budget bandwidth and capacity first

Decode is usually limited by these. Fill in:

required bandwidth = (weights + batch × KV per user) ÷ step time

required capacity = weights + batch × KV per user

Step 5. Choose numerics

Pick the narrowest format your models tolerate, then compute total bytes again.

Step 6. Choose array width and count

Width from the smallest K you care about. Count from required throughput ÷ (clock × width²). Check area and power.

Step 7. Size the on-chip memory

From tile size, double buffering, fusion and staging. Check bank bandwidth at each array edge.

Step 8. Size the feeders

Vector throughput, DMA queue depth (bandwidth × latency), scalar control. Check cycle tyranny.

Step 9. Choose parallelism, then network

Decide S and P from capacity and latency. Compute network bandwidth from all-reduce rates. Pick a topology from your traffic.

Step 10. Close the physical budget

Area, perimeter, power, cooling, yield. Identify what binds. Iterate.

Step 11. Search around your answer

Change several things at once. Bloat protects bloat, and savings compound through 1/x: two changes that each make something 2× cheaper can make it 100× cheaper together if costs are nearly gone. R A model will be wrong, but it will show you options and sensitivities. R

Example 1: a datacenter decode system

Goal. Serve a dense 70B model in FP8. 80 layers, 8 KV groups, width 128, 8K context. 50 tokens per second per user, with 256 users per system.

Step time. 1 ÷ 50 = 20 ms.

Weights. 70 GB. Reading them each step needs 3.5 TB/s.

KV. Per user: 2 × 80 × 8192 × 8 × 128 × 1 = 1.34 GB. For 256 users: 344 GB. Reading it each step: 17.2 TB/s.

So KV traffic is five times weight traffic. That is the main finding. Batching makes weights cheap per token and has no effect on KV.

Compute. 2 × 70B × 256 × 50 = 1.8 PFLOP/s. A modern accelerator's peak exceeds this.

Intensity. 2 × 70e9 × 256 FLOPs per step, over 70e9 + 344e9 bytes: about 87 FLOP/byte. That sits well under any modern ridge point, so this system is memory-bound. The array is not the problem.

Sizing, with Ironwood-class parts. Bandwidth: 20.7 TB/s ÷ 7.3 TB/s ≈ 3 chips. Capacity: 414 GB ÷ 206 GB (192 GiB) ≈ 2 chips, before any headroom. Use 4 for margin. Bandwidth binds first and capacity is close behind, which suggests this kind of part suits this workload fairly well.

Network. X = 8192 × 256 × 2 bytes = 4.2 MB per all-reduce, with 2 per layer, so 160 per step. At P=4 that is about 1 GB per step, or 50 GB/s per chip. Ironwood has 600 GB/s. Easy.

Now change one thing. Double the context to 16K. KV doubles to 688 GB, and needs 34 TB/s. You need about 6 chips, and compute is unchanged. Long context is a memory purchase.

What would a better design change? Sparse attention would cut that KV traffic. GQA with 4 groups would halve it. 4-bit KV would halve it again. Each of those is worth more here than any array improvement.

Example 2: an edge device

Goal. A 3B model at 4 bits on a phone-class chip with 68 GB/s LPDDR, one user.

Weights. 1.5 GB. Bandwidth limit: 68 ÷ 1.5 = 45 tokens per second at batch 1.

Compute. 2 × 3e9 × 45 = 270 GFLOP/s. A 32×32 array at 500 MHz gives 1 TOP/s, which is plenty.

Finding. This chip's job is mostly memory interface. The array can be tiny. Speculative decoding gives more reuse for one user, so more of the bandwidth works. R Even batch 4 is much more efficient than batch 1, and speculation and parallel agents can supply it. R

What not to build. A big array. Fancy sparsity. A wide NoC. Spend effort on memory efficiency and compression.

Example 3: a tiny embedded model

See Your chip. It gives the opposite conclusion: all weights fit on chip, so bandwidth is cheap, and the shape of the problem drives everything.

Decision tables

Which side of the roofline are you on?

If You are Spend on
Intensity ≪ ridge Memory-bound Bandwidth, compression, KV reduction
Intensity ≈ ridge Balanced Stop tuning this ratio
Intensity ≫ ridge Compute-bound Arrays, numerics, clock

Which limit binds first?

Symptom Binding limit Moves that help
Watts exceed cooling Power Wider and slower, lower voltage, narrower numerics
Area exceeds reticle Area Faster clock, multi-die, smaller SRAM
Perimeter exceeds PHY needs Beachfront Multi-die, stacked memory, chiplets
Array idle waiting on control Feeding 2D registers, queues, DMA feed
Array idle waiting on memory Bandwidth Larger tiles, fusion, more HBM
Array idle on small shapes Shape Smaller arrays, block-diagonal packing, heterogeneous cores
Latency too high at required batch Batch Faster network, more within-layer split, more weight bandwidth

The design review checklist

Before you trust a design, answer these.

  1. What is the target metric, and what is its denominator?
  2. What is the utilization on the smallest shape you must run?
  3. Is every queue sized by bandwidth × latency?
  4. What is the worst-case power pattern, and how fast can you throttle?
  5. How does yield survive one defect in the array?
  6. How do you test it at 2×2?
  7. What happens when software is worse than you assumed?
  8. Which number here is unmeasured?

Your chip

This chapter applies everything to your repo: pe.sv, sys_array.sv, tile_engine.sv and the embedded GPT-2 in PLAN.md. These are observations and suggestions. I have not changed your RTL, and I have not run synthesis. Every cycle count below comes from the analytical model, which matches TOTAL_CYCLES in your tile engine but is not a simulation of it.

What you have built, in this guide's terms

What you got right

Parametrization. Roune calls this a brilliant move he has not seen used anywhere: define everything by width, so you test at 2×2 and then scale. R ROWS, COLS, INNER_K, DATA_W and ACC_W already do this. Keep it up everywhere, including in your tests.

Output-stationary for a small design. Narrow moving data, simple dataflow, no weight-load path.

Wide accumulator with sign extension. ACC_W=32 is safe to K = 65,536.

A cycle model you can check. Your TOTAL_CYCLES comment matches the theory exactly.

The shape of your workload

The plan: 2 layers, d_model 64, 2 heads of width 32, FFN 256, vocab 256, context up to 32.

Operation M (decode) M (prefill) N K
QKV projection 1 32 192 64
Attention scores, per head 1 32 context 32
Attention values, per head 1 32 32 context
Output projection 1 32 64 64
FFN up 1 32 256 64
FFN down 1 32 64 256
LM head 1 32 256 64

Totals D: about 123,000 MACs per decoded token at context 32, and 114,688 bytes of weights plus embeddings. All of it fits on chip. So you are building a tiny version of a Groq-style machine: no DRAM, weights in on-chip memory, fully predictable. Your hardcoded FSM is literally static scheduling.

What array size should you pick?

The model's estimate of a full forward pass, with tiles running back to back: D

Array Decode cycles/token Decode util Prefill (32 tokens) cycles Prefill util
2×2 63,104 48.7% 1,009,664 97.4%
4×4 33,216 23.1% 265,728 92.5%
8×8 18,272 10.5% 73,088 84.1%
16×16 10,800 4.4% 21,600 71.1%
32×32 7,064 1.7% 7,064 54.4%

This table holds the main lesson.

Decode at M=1 wastes all but one row. From 8×8 to 16×16 you buy 4× the PEs and get 1.7× the decode speed. You are paying for rows with nothing to do.

Prefill behaves well. Larger arrays help a lot, because M=32 fills them.

Fill and drain dominate at small K. With K=64 on 32×32, the 62-cycle fill nearly doubles every tile. Overlapping tiles takes the 8×8 prefill from 84% to 99.6%.

So there is a real architectural choice here, and your plan says to test it. Report tokens per second, and report PE-count-normalized numbers too.

Fixing decode's M=1 problem

You have three options, and each teaches a concept from this guide.

Option 1: Split K across rows. Let each row of the array compute a partial dot product over a different K slice of the same output, then add those at the edge with a small reduction tree. This turns GEMV into full-array work. Your weights are on chip, so the bandwidth is cheap.

Option 2: Add a dedicated GEMV path. A row of MACs fed directly from wide SRAM, with a reduction tree. Roune's heterogeneous argument, at miniature scale.

Option 3: Batch or speculate. If you decode 4 streams at once, M=4 fills a 4×4 array. This changes your product, so it is a decision for you.

Things that will not scale past small arrays

None of these are bugs at 2×2. They become problems as ROWS and COLS grow.

1. The parallel output bus. ACC exposes R × C × 32 bits at once. At 16×16 that is 8,192 wires into whatever consumes them, which is the crossbar wiring problem from the fabric chapter. A real array shifts results out along columns, over R cycles. If you double-buffer the accumulator, that drain can overlap the next tile. This is probably your largest structural change.

2. Tile registers. A_reg and B_reg store the whole tile in flops. Replace them with banked SRAM feeding row and column FIFOs. For synthesis, flops cost several times what SRAM bits cost.

3. The skew mux. Each row selects A_reg[row][k_idx] through a mux that grows with INNER_K, driven by a shared counter. The usual structure is a triangular shift-register skew at the array edge, which needs no mux at all.

4. Global control. enable and clear_acc reach every PE in one cycle. At 16×16 that is a high-fanout net; at 256×256 it cannot meet timing. Pipeline these alongside the data, so that each PE gets its control when the wavefront arrives. A clear bit traveling with the first operand also removes the need to wait for a drain.

5. No tile overlap. The FSM runs IDLE → RUN → DONE → IDLE, so each tile pays fill, drain and handshake. To overlap, you need the next tile's skewed operands to follow immediately, with a double-buffered accumulator.

6. Accumulator width. Your largest K is 256, so 24 bits is enough, saving 8 flops of 48 per PE. Keep it as a parameter, and test it. That also shows you what saturation logic costs.

The surrounding blocks you will need

From your plan, and in this guide's terms:

Block Chapter Note
matmul_engine Shape Loop order decides what stays stationary. Keep accumulators across K tiles with init_acc=0, which you already support
Weight SRAM Memory 115 KB. Bank width should match array edge per cycle
KV cache Memory 2 layers × 2 × 32 × 64 = 8 KB at 1 byte per element
Requant Reduction Scale, shift, round, clip at the array edge, so 32-bit values never get stored
Softmax Vector Over at most 32 values. Use a small exp table, a reciprocal, and subtract the max first
LayerNorm Vector Needs reciprocal square root. Consider a small table plus a Newton step
GELU Vector A lookup table on int8 input has only 256 entries, which is exact and cheap
Controller Control Your static schedule is a strength. Add performance counters from day one

Nonlinear units and MoE designs these blocks in detail, and covers adding experts.

The GELU row is worth noticing. With int8 inputs, a 256-entry table is the exact function, and requires no approximation work at all. This trick does not exist at FP32.

Suggested experiments

Each answers a question this guide raises, with data you can produce in Verilator.

  1. Sweep R, C from 2 to 32. Reproduce the table above from RTL, and see how close the model is.
  2. Measure tile handshake overhead by comparing real cycles with K + R + C − 2.
  3. Add column-shift output and compare wiring and cycles.
  4. Add overlap, and check that you reach about 99% on 8×8 prefill.
  5. Try K-split for decode, and compare against the 10.5% baseline.
  6. Synthesize a PE with Yosys at 8, 16, 24 and 32-bit accumulators, and see where area goes.
  7. Sweep group size G (two or four multipliers per PE), and measure area per MAC.

Experiment 6 would give you real numbers for your target library. That would replace the O estimates in this guide with facts about your own chip.
